   Part I - Introduction 

 Background 

   

 1. This appeal comes directly to this Court from the High Court pursuant to Article 34.5.4⁰ of the Constitution following the grant of leave on 16 May 2025: see [2025] IESCDET 65. It arises from a judgment and Order of the High Court which quashed a decision of An Coimisiún Pleanála ("the Commission") of 23 August 2024. [1] By that decision the Commission refused to grant Coolglass Wind Farm Ltd. ("Coolglass"), planning permission in respect of a development of a 13-turbine wind farm and associated works in Timahoe, Co. Laois. The site itself lies some 2km from the Kilkenny border and is situated about 11km southeast of Portlaoise. 

 2. The significance of the appeal cannot be overstated, since it presents this Court with its first opportunity to consider the implications of s. 15(1) of the Climate Action and Low Carbon Development Act 2015 ("the 2015 Act") following important amendments made to that section effected by s. 17 of the Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Act 2021 ("the 2021 Act"). 

 3. The application by Coolglass was for a strategic infrastructure development, so it fell to be made directly to the Commission in the first instance under The Planning and Development Act 2000 as amended by The Planning and Development (Strategic Infrastructure) Act 2006. In its decision of 23 August 2024, the Commission had noted that the Laois County Development Plan 2021-2027 ("the development plan") was generally favourable to wind development. It concluded, however, that the proposed development by Coolglass would materially contravene objective CM RE 7 of the development plan . This prohibits the development of wind farms in " areas not open for consideration". The greater part of the actual site which is the subject of the application is located within such an excluded area. The Commission concluded that the proposed development would also contravene Policy Objective WES 7 of the Laois County Wind Energy Strategy which identified areas not considered suitable for windfarm development due to their overall sensitivity arising from landscape, ecological, recreational and/or cultural and built heritage resources. 

 4. In this respect the Commission expressly followed the approach that had been recommended by its Inspector in a report dated 16 May 2024. The Inspector had concluded that the development plan must take precedence over national climate policy saying (at para. 12.5.33) that national climate policy " cannot override the clear policy directives set by the County Development Plan ." The Inspector concluded (at para. 12.5.33) that national energy policies - while of considerable importance - " must be realised in a manner that respects local landscape sensitivities and planning policies ." 

 Summary of the High Court Judgment 

   

 5. Coolglass challenged this decision of the Commission in the High Court, succeeding on a number of grounds: see Coolglass Wind Farm Ltd. v An Bord Pleanála [2025] IEHC 1 . The central feature of the judgment revolved around the construction of s. 15(1) of the 2015 Act (as amended) ("Core Ground 1"). The High Court noted that this sub-section had itself been amended by the 2021 Act so that it now imposed a more elevated duty to perform functions of the Board (and other relevant bodies) (" so far as practicable.. . in a manner consistent with ") the most recently approved climate action plans ("CAPs") climate action strategy, national adaptation strategy and approved sectoral adaptation plans in furtherance of the national climate objective (defined by section 3(1) of the Act) and the " objective of mitigating greenhouse gas emissions and adapting to the effects of climate change in the State ." 

 6. The High Court - subject to a point which subsequently arose in relation to Core Ground 2 - accepted all of the evidence adduced by Coolglass, save where this was expressly disputed by the Commission (para. 15 of the judgment). That evidence was that the Climate Action Plan 2024 ("CAP 24") sets targets for wind energy including 9GW of onshore wind, 8GW of solar power and 80% share of renewables for the electricity market by 2030. Coolglass also emphasised that Ireland is " not on track " with regard to meeting its renewable energy targets, greenhouse gas emissions and broader climate plans and objectives. Finally, it urged that the proposed development at issue here comprises a renewable energy project with a total predicted output of some 85.8MW to 93.6MW which, if sanctioned by the grant of planning permission, would obviously contribute to the achievement of climate plans and objectives and would itself provide 1% of the total target contained in CAP 24. Indeed, the Commission's Inspector had concluded that the proposal would, if sanctioned, mean that when taken together with other wind energy projects currently operating in that county, County Laois would contribute nearly 1.5% of the total national output by 2030: see paragraph 11.2.3 of the Inspector's report. 

 7. In the course of a detailed examination of these legislative changes, the High Court concluded (at para. 72) that the amended Act " imposes sweeping obligations across the public sector from the Government down ." The judge reinforced this conclusion by reference to EU law considerations and (in the context of ss. 2 and 3 of the European Convention of Human Rights Act 2003) ("the 2003 Act") the decision of the European Court of Human Rights ("ECtHR") in Verein KlimaSeniorinnen Schweiz and Others v Switzerland [2024] ECHR 304 ([GC] No. 53600/20 9 April 2024) (" KlimaSeniorinnen" ). Noting that the Commission's decision did not mention s. 15(1) of the 2015 Act at all, the judgment concluded (at para. 150) that it had failed to act " consistently insofar as practicable with those goals and policies " contained in the 2015 Act. 

 8. In effect, the judge thus concluded that in view of the requirements of s. 15(1) of the 2015 Act, the Commission ought to have exercised its statutory powers under s. 37G(6) of The Planning and Development Act 2000 ("the 2000 Act") to grant permission in respect of this development, even though this would otherwise have represented a material contravention of the development plan. 

 9. In addition to the foregoing, it was accepted by all the parties that at one point in his report the Inspector fell into error by referring in this context to the wrong statutory provision empowering the Commission to depart from the provisions of the development plan (s. 37(2) of the 2000 Act) and that he ought to have referred instead to the Commission's somewhat more ample powers in this respect provided for in s. 37G(6) of that Act. Section 37(2) - as explained later in this judgment - applied when the Commission was dealing with an appeal from a planning authority, rather than determining an application for the first time. 

 10. The High Court took the view that had the correct and more permissive test in s. 37G(6) been applied by the Inspector, the Commission would have had greater freedom to depart from the terms of a development plan in order to comply with the requirements of s. 15(1) of the 2015 Act. The High Court concluded (at para. 46) that the "[ I ] nspector's report here is an utterly flawed document in key respects, even on the most orthodox and established administrative law basis ." 

 11. The High Court judge also appears to have concluded that the Commission had failed to act in a manner compatible with the requirements of the 2003 Act having regard to the manner in which Article 2 and Article 8 ECHR were interpreted by ECtHR in KlimaSeniorinnen : see paragraphs 151 to 153 of the judgment. 

 12. By order dated 14 March 2025, Humphreys J. granted an order of certiorari quashing the decision and remitting the matter to the Commission " to reconsider the application in accordance with the judgment ." 

 13.  While the judgment concluded that Coolglass was entitled to an order of certiorari on what might be termed standard judicial review grounds - including the invocation of the incorrect statutory provision and the taking into account of irrelevant considerations - the essence of the judgment, and its more wide-ranging significance, lay in its conclusion that the Commission was obliged by s. 15(1) of the 2015 Act to depart from the terms of a development plan in order to favour development which is more likely to enable Ireland to meet its climate change objectives unless it was impracticable to do so, and that this conclusion was reinforced by, and could be arrived at independently by, a consideration of European Union law and the recent decision of the ECtHR in KlimaSeniorinnen . The judgment set out a type of decision tree to be followed in applications for planning permission concerning projects which could be said to be contributing to limiting the effects of climate change such as the renewable energy project proposed by Coolglass. The principal argument against this interpretation is that the Oireachtas did not thereby intend that the structure and fabric of planning legislation - including the prohibitions contained in a development plan - could be so readily overridden in this way by the general words now found in s. 15(1) of the 2015 Act (as amended). 

 Part II - The Inspector's Report and the Commission's Decision 

   

 14.  In his report of 16 May 2024, the Commission's Inspector recommended the refusal of the permission, essentially on the ground that the proposed development was manifestly at odds with the existing development plan. As earlier noted, this conclusion is at the very core of this appeal, and it presents an issue which at once raises both standard administrative law arguments, on the one hand, as well as potentially far-reaching implications arising from the proper interpretation of s. 15(1) of the 2015 Act on the other. 

 15. The first thing to say about the Inspector's report is that it is an impressive document. In its own way, its very comprehensiveness bears eloquent testimony to the hugely complex nature of modern-day planning law. The Inspector nevertheless succeeded in producing a readable document running to over 240 pages which admirably traversed almost all of the relevant issues. It is true that in one respect the Inspector erred - or, it might be more accurate to say, was led into error by Coolglass's own submissions - in that, as already observed, he referred to the wrong section dealing with the Commission's power to contravene in a material respect the terms of the development plan. It is true, as will be discussed later in this judgment, that the Inspector also fell into serious error by not engaging sufficiently with the 2015 Act or, more particularly, the implications of the amendments made by the 2021 Act, especially in respect of s. 15(1). However, the inevitable focus on these issues and other aspects of the Inspector's report, in the unforgiving glare of robustly contested litigation, should not obscure the fact that overall, the report was an admirable one. It did not merit the criticism directed towards it in the judgment of the High Court, which in fairness to the High Court judge followed from conclusions in respect of the applicable law which, as will be seen, have not been upheld by this Court. 

 16. Following a detailed analysis of the application, the Inspector noted that the Laois County Development Plan sought to balance the development of renewables with the preservation of the character of the landscape. The Inspector noted that the proposed turbines had a ground-to-blade tip height of some 180m, so that they were (potentially) visible from a distance of some 20km: see paragraph 11.3.6 of the report. The site itself has an area of some 74 ha and encompasses an elongated area of some 6km in length. It straddles two hills, so that the site has elevations of between 196m to 325m. There are some 56 properties - generally one-off rural dwellings - within a 1km radius of the proposed development. The closest property is approximately 722m from one of the proposed wind turbines: see paragraphs 3.1.1 to 3.1.3 of the report. 

 17. The various policy objectives contained in the Development Plan had resulted in the demarcation of areas not open for consideration for wind farms, which objectives underscored what the Inspector described as (at para. 12.5.31) " a commitment to safeguard certain landscapes from development impacts that would significantly alter their appearance or character ." The Inspector ultimately concluded (at paras. 12.5.33 and 12.5.34) as follows:- 

 " It is my view that the overarching significance of the proposed development for renewable energy, economic development, and climate change mitigation cannot override the clear policy directives set by the County Development Plan. National energy policy and objectives, while critically important, must be realised in a manner that respects local landscape sensitivities and planning policies. To permit a development of this nature, which contravenes the explicit provisions of the Laois County Development Plan, would undermine the legitimacy of the Plan and the statutory planning process, setting an undesirable precedent for the future development of protected areas. 

 In the light of these considerations and taking into account the landscape and visual impact assessment presented in the [ Environmental Impact Assessment Report ] , I consider that the proposed wind farm, due to its location, would not only materially contravene the Laois County Development Plan but would also significantly impact the visual integrity and character of the landscape, which the Development Plan seeks to preserve. The Plan's policies and objectives reflect a deliberate prioritisation of landscape protection in areas not deemed suitable for wind farm development, a policy intent that must be upheld. " 

 18.  It is fair to say that the Inspector recommended the refusal of permission because it would significantly impact the visual integrity of the landscape, which was itself a key policy objective of the Development Plan, and was a factor in the designation of some areas as not open for consideration for wind farm developments. 

 19. The Inspector's analysis of the power of the Commission to depart from the terms of the development plan is dealt with at paragraphs 11.3.23-11.3.24 of his report:- 

 " The [ Commission ] will be aware that under section 37(2)(a) of the Planning and Development Act 2000, as amended, it may, in determining an appeal under that section, decide to grant permission even if the proposed development contravenes materially the Development Plan. This decision-making power is subject to the provisions of paragraph (b), which stipulates that the [ Commission ] may approve such developments under certain conditions: if the development is deemed strategically or nationally significant, if there are discrepancies or lack of clarity in the Development Plan's objectives regarding the project, if the development aligns with regional spatial and economic strategies, relevant government policies, or the statutory responsibilities of local authorities, or if it is consistent with the development trends and previous permissions in the area since the Development Plan was established. 

 In this instance, notwithstanding the Applicant's assertions of strategic importance and the imperatives of national energy policy, the compelling weight of evidence regarding the unsuitability of the site for wind farm development based on established policy provisions, significant visual impact, and landscape sensitivity, as well as oversight by the OPR and Ministerial Direction in 2022 is overwhelming. The proposed development not only challenges the integrity of the Laois County Development Plan but also raises substantive concerns about the precedent it sets for future developments within protected and sensitive areas. Therefore, considering all these factors and maintaining alignment with the principles of proper planning and sustainable development, I recommend refusing permission for the proposed development ." 

 20.  The High Court judgment commented on this, saying (at paras. 35 and 36):- 

 " It is confounding that the [ I ] nspector referred to 'an appeal' when he was dealing with a first-instance decision, and that he treated the application as being made under a section that obviously did not apply - and indeed that the erroneous reference to s. 37(2) was [ not ] picked up expressly by anybody subsequently. Admittedly the way the [ I ] nspector phrased the matter suggested that he got the wrong reference from within the applicant's material, but the [ Commission ] has to be able to do better than fly on automatic pilot and copy-and-paste mistakes into its decision-making documents. Plus, he does [ not ] claim to have got the utterly inappropriate word 'appeal' from the applicant. This is not a mere technicality ." 

 21. Section 37(2) of the 2000 Act (which it should be said does not apply) provides:- 

 " (a) Subject to paragraph (b) , the [ Commission ] may in determining an appeal under this section decide to grant a permission even if the proposed development contravenes materially the development plan relating to the area of the planning authority to whose decision the appeal relates. 

 (b) Where a planning authority has decided to refuse permission on the grounds that a proposed development materially contravenes the development plan, the [ Commission ] may only grant permission in accordance with paragraph (a) where it considers that 

 (i) the proposed development is of strategic or national importance, 

 (ii) there are conflicting objectives in the development plan or the objectives are not clearly stated, insofar as the proposed development is concerned, or 

 (iii) permission for the proposed development should be granted having regard to regional spatial and economic strategy for the area, guidelines under section 28, policy directives under section 29, the statutory obligations of any local authority in the area, and any relevant policy of the Government, the Minister or any Minister of the Government, or 

 (iv) permission for the proposed development should be granted having regard to the pattern of development, and permissions granted, in the area since the making of the development plan. 

 (c) Where the [ Commission ] grants a permission in accordance with paragraph (b) , the [ Commission ] shall, in addition to the requirements of section 34(10), indicate in its decision the main reasons and considerations for contravening materially the development plan ." 

 22. By contrast, the High Court judgment noted that s. 37G(6) of the 2000 Act (which does apply) simply provides:- 

 "(6) The [ Commission ] may decide to grant a permission for development, or any part of a development, under this section even if the proposed development, or part thereof, contravenes materially the development plan relating to any area in which it is proposed to situate the development." 

 23. The key difference between the two provisions is that the specific conditions which must be satisfied in the case of the exercise of the s. 37(2) power by the Commission are not present when it comes to the exercise of the s. 37G(6) power. 

 Part III - The Case Made by Coolglass 

   

 24. In order to understand the issues arising in this appeal, it is necessary next to summarise in general terms the case made by way of challenge to the Commission's decision. Coolglass had originally challenged the Commission's decision on seven core grounds. They are as follows: Core Ground 1: 

 The Commission had failed in its obligations under s. 15(1) of the 2015 Act. Core Ground 2: 

 The Commission had failed to properly exercise its jurisdiction under s. 37G(6) and/or s. 37(2)(b) of the 2000 Act to grant a planning permission which amounted to a material contravention of the development plan and/or had fettered its discretion in adopting a policy of refusing to exercise its discretion to do so in cases concerning wind farm development in areas designated unfavourable for wind farm development. Core Ground 3: 

 The Commission had purported to abdicate its obligations under s. 15 of the 2015 Act either to the Office of the Planning Regulator ("OPR") and/or the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage ("the Minister"). Core Ground 4: 

 The Commission erred by placing reliance on s. 37(2) of the 2000 Act instead of s. 37G(6) of the 2000 Act. Both statutory provisions deal with the power of the Commission to depart from the terms of a development plan, but, as already explained, the discretion conferred by the latter provision is more extensive than that which obtains in the case of the former provision. It is accepted that the Commission erred in referring to the wrong statutory provision and, on appeal, part of the debate was the extent to which this (by now admitted error) vitiated the validity of the decision. 

 Core Ground 5: 

 The Commission failed to exercise its functions in a manner which was compatible with Article 2 and Article 8 ECHR in accordance with s. 3 of the 2003 Act in the light, in particular, of the decision in KlimaSeniorinnen. 

 25. Coolglass also relied on two specific EU law grounds as core grounds: Core Ground 6: 

 The Commission failed to treat the proposed development as being in the overriding public interest and serving public health and safety and to give priority to that overriding public interest as required by Article 3(2) of Regulation (EU) 2022/2577 laying down a framework to accelerate the deployment of renewable energy. Core Ground 7: 

 The Commission breached the duty of sincere cooperation in Article 4(3) TEU by refusing to exercise its discretion under s. 37G(6) and/or s. 37(2)(b) of the 2000 Act to grant permission for the development, thereby jeopardising the attainment of the objectives of the EU, including the binding obligations of the European Union and its Member States with respect to climate change. 

 Relevant Legislative Provisions 

   

 26. Since it is of key significance for the present case, it is convenient to set out s. 15(1) of the 2015 Act (as substituted by s. 17 of the 2021 Act. It now provides:- 

 "(1) A relevant body shall, in so far as practicable, perform its functions in a manner consistent with 

 (a) the most recent approved climate action plan, 

 (b) the most recent approved national long term climate action strategy, 

 (c) the most recent approved national adaptation framework and approved sectoral adaptation plans, 

 (d) the furtherance of the national climate objective, and 

 (e) the objective of mitigating greenhouse gas emissions and adapting to the effects of climate change in the State " (emphasis added). 

 The language highlighted was introduced for the first time by the 2021 Act. That Act also altered the plans and strategies in the subparagraphs, but for present purposes nothing turns on these alterations which were made to make the section consistent with the terms of the 2021 Act. Of more importance is the definition of " relevant body " which adopts by reference the definition of public body and prescribed body contained in the Freedom of Information Act of 2014. The definition of public body in section 6 of the latter Act is very wide indeed. It includes a Department of State; any entity, other than a company, established by a Minister either directly or under a scheme; a company the majority of shares in which are held by or on behalf of a Minister; an institution of higher education in receipt of public funding; parent bodies, subsidiaries or related entities and any body which was a public body for the purposes of the Freedom of Information Act 1997. If this was not comprehensive enough the Minister also had power to prescribe bodies for the purpose of the 2014 Act, having the consequence that they would also become relevant bodies for the purposes of the 2015 Act as amended. The Act thus applies across the public sector generally. 

 27.  It is accepted that the Commission (and any local authority) is a " relevant body " for the purpose of this section. Part IV - The Judgment of the High Court 

   

 28. As already noted, the High Court delivered a comprehensive judgment in favour of Coolglass and quashed by certiorari the decision by the Commission to refuse to grant Coolglass planning permission for this development. While the judgment does not admit of easy summary, it is nonetheless helpful to break down its individual components. 

 29. The High Court found (paras. 47 to 51) that the Commission had regard to irrelevant considerations by relying on the fact that neither the OPR nor the Minister had objected to the relevant provisions of the development plan in the procedure provided for under s. 31 of the 2000 Act (i.e. Core Ground 3). The judge also found that the Commission had incorrectly relied on s. 37(2)(b) of the 2000 Act, rather than s. 37G(6) (paras. 30 to 46) and that this error of law meant that it had not properly exercised its discretion in this regard (Core Ground 4). While the High Court acknowledged that the case could have been decided in Coolglass's favour on these two grounds alone, he concluded that (at para. 52) " it is for the best if I decide all of the other grounds ." (In the event this did not include Core Ground 2 for reasons which will be addressed presently). In the light of the decision on these matters on this appeal, this was a helpful, indeed correct, course - it would be obviously unsatisfactory if these matters were decided in a piecemeal fashion, particularly because of the wide-ranging nature of the claims made by Coolglass. In consequence the judgment set out conclusions of law that, if upheld, would have far reaching implications for both the planning process and administrative law more generally, and it is desirable that such matters should be addressed and resolved as soon as possible. Core Ground 1: The Interpretation of s. 15(1) of the 2015 Act 

   

 30. Critically, however, the Court also found against the Commission in respect of Core Ground 1 (the construction of s. 15(1) of the 2015 Act). It was noted that Ireland was not on course to meet its renewable energy targets. In these circumstances the Court concluded (at para. 131) that the Commission:- 

 " must ask itself what substantive disposition of the matter that is practicably available would contribute to achieving the s. 15 goals. In the case of renewable energy projects, the answer to that will almost always be a grant of permission, and is obviously so here " (emphasis added). 

 The judgment went on to record (at para. 131) that the Commission:- 

 "... should then ask whether the substantive disposition of the matter in a way that furthers climate goals is precluded by a mandatory and non-fixable legal requirement that confers no discretion or evaluative judgement on the decision-maker. If so, the project has to be refused no matter how climate-friendly it is. 

 (iii) If the answer to that is No, the [ Commission ] should then ask if its discretion or evaluative judgement can be exercised in such a way as to support the outcome favouring climate goals. Examples include the following: 

 (a) insofar as concerns an overall judgement as to proper planning and sustainable development, that must be exercised in an evaluative way that furthers climate goals if practicable, albeit that it could allow the [ Commission ] to form an independent judgement that a project did not comply with the principles of proper planning and sustainable development, if those two concepts are properly considered together; 

 (b) insofar as concerns material contravention, if such contravention arises, the [ Commission ] should exercise the power to permit such contravention in whatever way that furthers climate goals if practicable to do so - as the applicant submits, the [ Commission ] cannot merely defer to a limitation in an individual development plan if to do so would contribute to an inconsistency (the avoidance of which is not impracticable) with climate plans and objectives contrary to s. 15; 

 (c) if non-mitigable impacts on European sites arise, the [ Commission ] must apply the public interest override in a manner that furthers climate goals, if practicable to do so; and 

 (d) if there is some impracticability in a grant of permission, but it can (or could potentially) be resolved by a procedural decision that is not impracticable, then the [ Commission ] is required to make the procedural decision that is most consistent with climate goals to enable the problem to be fixed - for example to require further information or to carry out any additional steps open to it regarding assessments if the developer's initial assessment information is deemed inadequate. 

 I do need to emphasise that the obligation to use discretionary powers favourably to renewable energy infrastructure does not automatically translate into an obligation to refuse permission for developments that cause emissions. One can see an argument as to why the [ Commission ] would not be required to start from a position of scepticism in relation to projects causing emissions to quite the same extent as it should start from a presumption of favourability regarding renewable projects. We can save detailed consideration for a case in which it arises but there are two obvious reasons for this : 

 (i) The concept of  net  zero implies a continuing necessity for some emissions in the short term at least. That relates to the fact that pending complete adaptation of the economy, there will be other imperatives of economic necessity that require projects that, in and of themselves, would [ not ] support climate goals in isolation. Energy security to enable the ongoing orderly functioning of society, especially in the context of the Russian Federation's full-scale criminal war of aggression against Ukraine, is one example. 

 (ii) Even if a project is not in itself driven by such an imperative, one has to be conscious of displacement effects. Refusal of a project in Europe may simply have the effect of the project being relocated to a jurisdiction with lower environmental standards, thus producing more emissions overall. Emissions are definitionally a cumulative global problem, so while refusing such projects feels good in the moment, it may or may not be doing anything to combat climate change. Rightly or wrongly, that was an explicit part of my thinking in  An Taisce v. An Bord Pleanála   [2021] IEHC 254 ... Such an approach does [ not ] particularly give one a feeling of virtue, but it makes a certain amount of sense depending on the context." 

 31.   Humphreys J. observed (at para. 133) that it did not:- 

 " automatically follow from a pro-renewables interpretation that there must be, say, an anti-cheese factory interpretation, an anti-data centre interpretation or an anti-LNG storage interpretation. The trade-offs and displacement effects would need to be considered. " 

 He concluded that the Commission had simply failed to engage with its s. 15(1) obligations. 

   

   

   Core Ground 5 - ECHR 

   

 32.  Coolglass had submitted that a similar conclusion followed when regard was had to the provisions of the ECHR (Core Ground 5). In this context, the High Court judge referred (at paras. 103-108) to ss. 2 and 4 of the ECHR Act and the decision of the ECtHR in KlimaSeniorinnen. He then concluded (at paras. 109-113) that he agreed with Coolglass that:- 

 "... one must conclude that art. 8 of the ECHR imposes a positive obligation on the State to put in place a legislative and administrative framework with respect to climate change designed to provide effective protection of human health and life, and a further positive obligation to apply that framework effectively in practice, and in a timely manner. 

 Ireland has a framework of course but... it is clear that it is not being complied with. The latter failure, on the logic of  KlimaSeniorinnen , involves a breach of art. 8 of the ECHR. 

 The application of the framework in practice is crucial. As we know from the termination of pregnancy context ( Case of A, B and C v. Ireland  [GC], no. 25579/05, ECHR 2010), the Strasbourg court takes a dim view of a situation where there are laws on the books but a failure to put in place practical arrangements to implement them. 

 The problem for the opposing parties here is firstly that an interpretation of s. 15(1) that allows the climate goals in legislation to fall by the wayside due to a failure by the [ Commission ] to exercise discretionary powers to override development plans is an interpretation that fails to conform with ECHR obligations contrary to s. 2 of the 2003 Act. 

 Secondly, the failure by the [ Commission ] to use its discretionary powers in that manner constitutes a failure to act consistently with ECHR obligations contrary to s. 3 of the 2003 Act ." 

 33.  Humphreys J. further stated (at paras. 114 and 115) that the Commission:-

 Part V - Summary of the Position of the Parties in Respect of the Principal Arguments 

 Section 15 of the 2015 Act (Core Grounds 1, 3 and 4, but Especially Core Ground 1) 

   

 41.  This issue is at the heart of the appeal. Section 15(1) of the 2015 Act originally provided that a relevant body was required to " have regard to " the climate standards. A new version of s. 15(1) was inserted by s. 17 of the 2021 Act. This provides that a relevant body " shall, in so far as practicable , perform its functions in a manner consistent with " certain Climate Plans and Objectives, including CAP 24 and recent national long term climate action strategies (emphasis added). In this way, s. 15(1) imposes a qualified obligation to act consistently with these climate obligations. Relevant bodies are also obliged to exercise their functions with reference to the objective of mitigating greenhouse gas emissions. 

 42. The general approach of both the Commission and the State parties is to say that these statutory " as far as practicable " and " consistency " obligations imposed by s. 15(1) must be understood in their appropriate context and, specifically, that they cannot be understood as imposing a specific obligation on the Commission to derogate from accepted norms (such as the generally binding character of development plans) prescribed by the general system contained in the Planning Acts. The Commission draws attention to the fact that the Oireachtas had clearly elected not to effect any amendments to either s. 37G(6) and/or s. 37(2) of the 2000 Act. Here the Commission points to the presumption against unclear changes in the law and the maxim generalia specialibus non derogant . 

 43. The State parties take a similar view, arguing that if the High Court's approach were to be followed, this would give rise to what they described as a strong, almost overriding, presumption that permissions for developments causing emissions should be refused and that this would have grave and far-reaching implications for many important public interest projects. While the State parties accept that the Commission is under a qualified consistency obligation, they say that this does not have the effect of transforming such discretionary powers into an obligation either to reach a particular outcome or very strong presumptions to that effect in the manner suggested by the High Court. 

 44. The State parties also contend that s. 15 cannot be interpreted in a manner which would undermine the integrity of the planning system generally, either by creating de facto presumptions in favour of or against the grant of permissions in respect of particular developments or by undermining the entire system of development plans. The State parties reject the suggestion that they had ever contended that development plans automatically supersede other obligations on planning authorities. They nonetheless point to decisions such as Spencer Place Development Company Ltd. v Dublin City Council [2020] IECA 268 (per Collins J. at paras. 10 and 28) to demonstrate that development plans cannot be lightly displaced or disregarded in the planning process. 

 45. So far as the general " consistency " obligation is concerned, the Commission and the State Parties point by analogy to the decision of this Court in Killegland Estates v Meath County Council [2023] IESC 39 where the statutory obligation contained in s. 12(18) of the 2000 Act to ensure that a development plan was " consistent " with the objectives of the National Planning Framework was found (at para. 102) to mean " consistent generally, as distinct from complying in every detailed and minor particular ." It says that the same applies to compliance with CAP 24 and the other climate action plans. 

 46. For its part, Coolglass maintains that the:- 

 " fundamental premise of the [ Commission ] Decision - that national climate policy cannot override an express prohibition in the Development Plan - represents a clear legal error in the Commission's interpretation and application of its obligations. " 

 It goes on to address (Coolglass submissions at para. 8) the Commission's consistency obligations:- 

 "... the obligation of consistency , to be achieved insofar as practicable, imposed by Section 15 of the 2015 Act must necessarily take precedence over the obligation in section 37G of the 2000 Act to consider the Development Plan when determining an application for permission under section 37G... In concluding that national climate policy cannot override an express prohibition in the Development Plan, the Commission incorrectly reversed that hierarchy ." 

 47. Coolglass further points to the fact that the obligations contained in s. 15 of the 2015 Act were considerably strengthened and augmented by the 2021 Act. It says that the Oireachtas in enacting these provisions intended to bring about a transformative shift in how Ireland addresses the climate crisis and to create an effective and enforceable framework for action. It relies on recent decisions of this Court in Heather Hill v An Bord Pleanála [2022] IESC 43 , [2022] 2 ILRM 313 and Delaney v Personal Injuries Assessment Board [2024] IESC 10 in support of its argument that the statutory context is often highly relevant:- 

 " in determining the obligation on relevant bodies under section 15 of the 2015 Act to act in a manner that is ' consistent ' so far as ' practicable ' with the Climate Plans and Objectives, and also in determining the obligation on the Commission to ' consider ' the Development Plan when determining applications for permission... under section 37G of the 2000 Act. " 

 Core Grounds 5 and 7 - The ECtHR Judgment in KlimaSeniorinnen and Conforming Interpretation of EU Law 

   

 48. Both the Commission and the State parties observe that it is not suggested that s. 15(1) of the 2015 Act gives effect to any specific EU law obligations. In these circumstances, they both contend that there is no obligation to adopt a conforming interpretation of this provision. While Humphreys J. had stated (at para. 117) that " all vectors of interpretation point strongly in the same direction " so that an " imperative " interpretation of s. 15 is required, these parties contend that the judgment does not identify the basis for such a conforming interpretation.

It points to a variety of EU agreements and instruments (set out at para. 95 of the High Court judgment) which it says require this conforming interpretation. 

 50. While the High Court judgment also raises questions regarding the true effect and interpretation of the ECtHR's judgment in KlimaSeniorinnen, specifically having regard to ss. 2 and 3 of the 2003 Act, the State parties maintain that having regard to the terms of the 2003 Act there was no proper basis on which the High Court could have made such a finding. In addition, they maintain that there are questions as to the extent to which a limited company could rely on Article 8 ECHR dealing with family life.

These parties also draw attention to the fact that this Court has already ruled in Friends of the Irish Environment v Government of Ireland [2020] IESC 49 , [2021] 3 IR 1 (" Friends of the Irish Environment" ) that a litigant in an environmental claim of this kind must demonstrate that they have been affected by the impugned measure. Coolglass notes that in KlimaSeniorinnen the ECtHR held that Contracting States were obliged by Article 8 ECHR to put in place a legislative and administrative framework designed to provide effective protection of human health and life, as well as being subject to a further positive obligation to apply that framework effectively in practice. The State parties observe in response that it is not clear how the KlimaSeniorinnen duty to put in place a legislative and administrative framework has the effect of requiring an interpretation of s. 15(1) of the 2015 Act in a manner that requires the existing development plan to be overridden, at least on a presumptive basis. 

 The Interpretation of s.15 of the 2015 Act (as amended) 

 53. The interpretation of s. 15(1) of the 2015 Act as amended by the 2021 Act is the central issue in the case. The relevant sections of the Inspector's report have already been set out at paragraphs 17-19, and the portions of the High Court judgment dealing with this issue are set out above at paragraphs 30-31. The parties' positions on this issue are summarised at paragraphs 41-47. It is necessary now however to consider in some detail the question of the proper interpretation and application of s. 15(1) (as amended) particularly in the field of planning decisions, since that is the critical issue of wide general public importance that has given rise to this appeal. 

 54. The principal dispute in this issue is between Coolglass and the State parties. The Commission, while arguing that the approach of the High Court was wrong, expressed itself as being content to seek guidance from the Court as the interpretation of this section will apply to the Commission in the performance of its functions. It acknowledged that this was a difficult question. Coolglass and the State parties took sharply contrasting positions on this interpretive issue and then sought to attack an exaggerated version of the opposing argument in the hope, perhaps, that a rejection of an extreme version of the opposing argument would by default lead to the acceptance of the opposite (albeit correspondingly extreme) interpretation. It is not possible to accept either argument fully and it is necessary therefore to analyse particularly carefully the underlying material, and the arguments of the parties, in order to arrive at what the Court considers is the correct interpretation of s 15(1) and its application to this case. 

   The Section 

 55. Section 15(1) of the 2015 Act (as amended) has already been set out at paragraph 26 above, but the fact of its amendment by the Act of 2021 is itself a relevant consideration in this case. In its original terms as enacted in 2015, the section provided as follows:- 

             "(1) A relevant body shall, in the performance of its functions, have regard to 

             (a) the most recent approved national mitigation plan, 

 (b) the most recent approved national adaptation framework and approved sectoral adaptation plans, 

             (c) the furtherance of the national transition objective, and 

 (d) the objective of mitigating greenhouse gas emissions and adapting to the effects of climate change in the State." 

 56. The contrast with the amendments introduced by the 2021 Act is obvious, and the direction of travel is clear. Thus, s. 15(1) now provides:- 

 " (1) A relevant body shall, in so far as practicable , perform its functions in a manner consistent with  

             (a) the most recent approved climate action plan, 

             (b) the most recent approved national long term climate action strategy, 

 (c) the most recent approved national adaptation framework and approved sectoral adaptation plans, 

             (d) the furtherance of the national climate objective, and 

 (e) the objective of mitigating greenhouse gas emissions and adapting to the effects of climate change in the State" (emphasis added). 

 57. This then is the provision which applied to the decision of the Commission in this case. The thrust of the amendments made in 2021 to s. 15 is clear: they undoubtedly strengthen the obligation created in 2015 by changing a requirement that the relevant body " have regard to " the most up to date climate objectives, to an obligation to perform its functions " in a manner consistent with " those climate objectives " in so far as practicable ". Both parties agreed that the Commission was a " relevant body " for the purposes of the Act, and that s. 15(1) clearly applied to it, when exercising its functions both in relation to planning applications and considering the exercise of its power to grant permission even if the proposed development contravened materially the development plan relating to the area, whether pursuant to s. 37(2) or s. 37G(6). The grant or refusal of permission is the function of a relevant body, and must therefore be performed consistently with the climate objectives now set out in s. 15(1). 

 58. While s. 15(1) loomed large in the High Court judgment, and even more centrally in this appeal, it was not initially the focus of the same degree of attention in the planning process, and there is a mismatch between the importance attributed to s. 15(1) (as amended) in these proceedings, in this appeal, and the role it played in the planning application and process. 

 59. It appears that it did not figure at all in the consultation between Coolglass and the Commission under s. 37B of the Planning and Development Act 2000 (as amended) which consultation is a necessary precursor to the acceptance by the Commission of a proposed development as a strategic infrastructure development. Nor did it figure at least in express terms, in the voluminous planning application itself. The first reference by Coolglass to s. 15(1) appears in a single compendious document of 20 December 2023, in which Coolglass's representative set out its response to the third party observations which had been submitted to the Commission in respect of the application. 

 60. In respect of the contention made that the development would be a material contravention of the Laois Development Plan, Coolglass referred to the proposed development first in terms of European policy explaining that it was a renewable energy plant and therefore was a project of " overriding public interest " as set out in the REPowerEU Plan of May 2022 and the revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III) adopted on 18 October 2023. Under that Directive, there was a presumption that renewable energy plants were of overriding public interest except where there was clear evidence that the project had significant adverse effects on the environment. The response also went on to refer to the National Climate Action Plan of 2023 and then, and subsequently, referred to s. 15 of the Act (as amended) stating less than forcefully: "this clearly places the onus on ABP [ the Commission ] to assess applications in accordance with National Policy" . The submission on this entire aspect concluded in somewhat general terms:- 

 "it is requested that [ the Commission ] have due regard to the European and National legislation when examining the Laois wind energy strategy and exercise its discretion under Section 37(2)(b) of the Planning and Development Act (as amended)" . 

 It will be noted that this is the source of the mistaken reference to s. 37(2)(b) rather than s. 37G(6). 

 61. This lack of direct connection to the detail of this case means that the issue has been addressed at a somewhat theoretical level. It would have been more helpful if there was a closer focus on the manner in which it was said the section should take effect in the present case. However, while reliance on s. 15(1) could have been more forceful and explicit, there is no doubt that the thrust of Coolglass's submission to the Commission was, insomuch as it could be considered, that the proposed development contravened the Laois Development Plan and the Commission should exercise its power to grant permission, notwithstanding the fact that it would amount to a material contravention of the plan, because of the climate benefits of the project, and the fact that it was to that extent consistent with national policy. Section 15(1) was therefore engaged. It was accepted by all parties that s. 15(1) applied to the Commission's exercise of its functions. The dispute, which generated much contention, was precisely how s. 15(1) was to apply to the case. 

 62. The Commission's decision referred to Policy Objective CM RE 5 of the Laois County Development Plan 2021-2027, which sought to facilitate wind energy development in accordance with guidelines for planning authorities and wind energy development, and noted that Policy Objective CM RE 7 prohibited the location of wind farms in areas identified as "not open for consideration ". Accordingly, the Commission considered, having regard to the totality of relative policy in relation to wind energy as set out in the statutory plan, that the proposed development would materially contravene objective CM RE 7 and policy objective WES 7 (Wind Energy Strategy) and would therefore be contrary to the proper planning and sustainable development of the area. 

 63. In this regard, the Commission was following the reasoning set out in the Inspector's report. The Inspector noted (at page 49) the local authority's submission that the development was considered to materially contravene the Laois Development Plan "thus contrary to proper planning and sustainable development in the area" . The Inspector's own assessment (para. 12.5.30) expressed the view that the proposed development's location within an area designated as "not open for consideration" represented a "fundamental conflict with the planning policy framework" . 

 64. The Inspector concluded that (para 12.5.33):- 

 "The overarching significance of the proposed development for renewable energy, economic development and climate change mitigation cannot override the clear policy directives set by the County Development Plan. National energy policy and objectives, while critically important, must be realised in a manner that respects local landscape sensitivities and planning policies. To permit a development of this nature, which contravenes the explicit provisions of the Laois County Development Plan, would undermine the legitimacy of the Plan and the statutory planning process, setting an undesirable precedent for the future development of protected areas." 

        Accordingly, the Inspector concluded that (para. 12.5.35):- 

 "Notwithstanding the potential benefits associated with renewable energy development, the proposal in its current location would materially contravene the Laois County Development Plan 2021-2027 and its appendaged Wind Energy Strategy ... and thereby would be contrary to the proper planning and sustainable development of the area." 

 65. The High Court judgment in this regard has already been set out (at paras. 30-31) and can therefore be summarised as expressing a strong presumption in favour of the grant of permission in respect of a climate friendly project such as this. The consistency standard introduced to s. 15 in 2021 was a high and demanding standard, and " practicability " meant "capable of being put into practice, not merely doing what is reasonable [ and was ] a very high standard only just falling short of unconditional compliance requirements." The conclusion was summarised at paragraph 131 that in a case such as this, the Commission:- 

 "must ask itself what substantive disposition of the matter that is practicably available would contribute to achieving the s. 15 goals. In the case of renewable energy projects, the answer to that will almost always be a grant of permission, and is obviously so here" . 

 The High Court judgment (at para. 131, and set out in detail at para. 30 above) set out a form of decision tree showing a strong disposition in favour of the grant of permission for any project which could be said to contribute to the achievement of the s. 15 goals. It appeared to create almost a new system for the consideration of planning applications at least in respect of carbon reducing projects. The judgment did acknowledge that this approach did not operate in exactly the same way in the obverse situation i.e. where an application for permission for a project creating emissions was being considered. This was because of two factors. First, that the concept of net zero and the necessity of some emissions in the short term at least, and second, that a planning body had to be conscious of displacement effects. 

 66. The State parties argued that the provisions of s. 15 as amended in 2021 operated at the general level of State policy and that " these measures and objectives are of a general and programmatic character and are not intended to supplant or predetermine decision-making in individual cases" (para. 37 of the State's submissions). The State parties and the Commission also maintained that insomuch as s. 15 had application in the context of planning permissions at all, then decisions made by planning authorities as to what was or was not consistent with climate objectives and/or practicable or impracticable was to be judged by a deferential standard of rationality. It was said that it was for the Commission (or where relevant a planning authority) to decide if any project was consistent with the s. 15 objectives, and/or if it was impracticable to grant permission, and a court would only set aside such a determination if it was irrational applying the standard set out in State ( Keegan) v The Stardust Compensation Tribunal [1986] IR 642. 

 67. While the State's contention that s. 15 does not predetermine a decision making in a particular case does not exclude the possibility that s. 15 may yet have effect upon that decision, the State parties struggled to explain how, consistent with their argument, s. 15, particularly if tested only by a rationality standard, could have a significant influence at that level. 

 68. Coolglass for its part adopted the approach of the High Court in this regard. It argued that the State parties consistently downplayed the existence of s. 15 (as amended) which Coolglass argued had far-reaching comprehensive obligations. In particular, there was a significant shift from a process requirement (" have regard to ") to an obligation of outcome (consistency). There were, it was said, three stages to compliance by the Commission with the duty imposed on it by s. 15(1). First, it is said the decision must make or must identify the particular plans and objectives with which the decision is to be consistent under s. 15. Second, those documents must be interpreted to understand what they require. Third, it is suggested that the decision maker must ask themselves what decision is consistent with the plans and objectives in question. In this case, that question is answered very easily insomuch as it is said that the grant of planning permission is plainly consistent with the climate objectives as enumerated in subparagraphs (a) to (e) of s. 15(1), and there is nothing impracticable in granting such a permission. 

 69. Coolglass did qualify the reasoning in the High Court judgment in one significant respect. Coolglass sought to refine the test somewhat by contending that 'impracticability', could contemplate legal as well as factual difficulties. Since planning authorities were obliged to act in accordance with proper planning and sustainable development under s. 34 of the Planning and Development Act 2000, and cannot act ultra vires , a development which would not be consistent with proper planning and sustainable development, would be impracticable in this sense, and therefore permission need not, indeed could not, be granted. On this approach, considerations of proper planning and sustainable development would be introduced into the application of the s. 15(1) " consistency " obligation. 

 70. This is a variant of the reasoning in paragraph 131 of the High Court judgment set out at paragraph 30 above. While it was suggested that there was a strong presumption in favour of the grant of permission, it was acknowledged that the considerations of proper planning and sustainable development could have the effect of leading to a refusal of a permission for renewable energy project albeit that must be approached "in an evaluative way that furthers climate goals" . 

 

 Analysis 

 71. Insomuch as there is a dispute between the parties as to the significance of s. 15(1) and the test to be applied when a court has to determine whether the obligation under s. 15(1) has been complied with, we are satisfied that the submissions of Coolglass are substantially more correct: s. 15(1) and in particular the amendments effected in 2021 are of real importance and effect; they impose an obligation not just of process but of outcome; and that outcome, if challenged, is not tested by a rationality standard, but rather by compliance or not with the legal obligation proposed. The reasons for our conclusions in this regard are also relevant to the proper interpretation of s. 15(1) and it is accordingly necessary to set them out in some detail. 

 72. Coolglass placed the amendments to s. 15(1) in the context of the other amendments to the 2015 Act effected by the 2021 Act. Coolglass argued, correctly in our view, that taken cumulatively, those changes demonstrated a clear legislative intention to upgrade and strengthen a number of " have regard to" provisions in the 2015 Act and replace them with obligations to act " consistently with " the s. 15 climate objectives. The effect of these changes it was argued, was, and was intended, to create binding legal obligations capable of being assessed and enforced by a court. It is true, that as originally enacted, s. 15 of the 2015 Act did create legal obligations which were enforceable, but it was argued that these obligations were of process, rather than outcome and a relevant body could comply with the relevant provisions in the 2015 Act by having regard to the State's climate action plans, but no more. The 2021 amendments required that the action of the relevant body meets a substantive outcome: it must be consistent so far as practicable with the climate objectives. 

 73. Coolglass also pointed to s. 3 of the Act (as substituted by s. 5 of the 2021 Act) which imposes an obligation on the State more generally to " pursue and achieve, by no later than the end of the year 2050, the transition to a climate resilient, biodiversity rich, environmentally sustainable and climate neutral economy (in this Act referred to as the 'national climate objective'" and to the provisions of s. 3(2) requiring the Minister to submit to the Government for approval carbon budgets, a sectoral emissions ceiling, a climate action plan, and a national long term climate action strategy together with a national adaptation framework. Section 3(3) also now imposes on the obligation on the Government to carry out its functions in a manner consistent with the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change of 1992, the Paris Agreement of 2015, and any mitigation or adaptation commitments entered into by the EU. These obligations are in addition to the general obligation imposed on Ministers themselves as relevant bodies under s. 15. Section 4(11) requires a Minister of the Government, so far as practicable, to perform their functions in a manner consistent with the most recent approved climate action plan and the most recent approved national long term action strategy. The overlap between all these provisions it was said, indicated a strong emphasis being placed on ensuring that all public functions were carried out in a manner consistent with climate objectives. 

 74. In addition, Coolglass also pointed to the s. 2A of the Act (also introduced in 2021) which provides:- 

 "For the avoidance of doubt no remedy or relief by way of damages or compensation is available with respect to or arising out of any failure, of whatever kind, to comply with any provision of this Act or any obligation or duty created thereunder." 

 Coolglass argued that this was a clear indication that the Act was intended and understood to have the effect of creating obligations enforceable in court, which in the absence of a saving provision such as s. 2A, were capable of extending to a claim for damages. If, it was argued, the Act did not create binding legal obligations, there would have been no reason to exclude the possibility of a damages claim. 

 75. Finally, Coolglass pointed to the general and overarching nature of s. 15 in creating duties which apply to all relevant bodies requiring them to carry out their functions in compliance with the section. Coolglass argued that the closest analogy to this type of provision was to be found in sections 2 and 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003, which imposes an obligation in interpreting and applying any statutory provision or rule of law and to do so in a manner compatible with the State's obligations under the Convention provisions (s. 2), and an obligation on every organ of the State to perform its functions in a manner compatible with the State's obligations under the Convention provisions (s. 3). This, it was said, was a clear indication of how far-reaching and comprehensive the obligations imposed by s. 15 are. Instead of a statute-by-statute amendment and enumeration of specific powers and duties, the Oireachtas had elected to impose a single overarching obligation on all relevant bodies. 

 76. In our view, these features of the Act, and in particular the amendments effected in 2021, all demonstrate a clear legislative intention to impose legal obligations on all relevant bodies constituting the machinery of the State. We are of the view, therefore, that Coolglass is correct insofar as it contends that the obligation under s. 15(1) cannot be simply reduced to a procedural obligation. If that were so, the amendments introduced by the 2021 Act would have had very limited, or perhaps no, real effect, and that was inconsistent with the introduction of such comprehensive and significant amendments. 

 77. Furthermore, we do not accept that compliance with s. 15 is to be tested by a standard of irrationality. Section 15 does not confer a general discretion on a relevant body. If it did, or if the question could be reduced to one of planning judgment, then the analysis in cases such as Sherwin v An Bord Pleanála [2024] IESC 13 , and Jennings v An Bord Pleanála [2023] IEHC 14 might arise. In this regard, it is important to keep in mind the central fact that s. 15 is not addressed itself, either exclusively or even principally, to planning authorities. It is directed to all relevant bodies, many of which may not have decision making functions in respect of individual cases. Section 15 is concerned with the performance of the functions of all such bodies, and in principle a court must be able to decide if the obligation has been complied with or not. As we will see later, that obligation of consistency does not however dictate a single result, and a range of decisions may be said to be consistent with the s. 15 objectives, particularly if the context of the plans with which consistency is to be assessed, is (as these are) stated at a level of generality. However, the decision of an authority must, to comply with s. 15, be capable of falling within that range. Whether or not it does so is a wholly objective question, and is a matter of law. 

 78. Accordingly, the question for any court when faced with a decision to a planning decision asserting non-compliance with s. 15 is whether the performance of the functions of the relevant body, and in the case of a planning authority, the decision to grant or not to grant a permission, or to grant a permission subject to conditions, falls within the spectrum of possible outcomes that could still be said to be consistent, in so far as is practicable, with the objectives of s. 15 stated as they are, at a level of considerable generality and by reference to plans themselves stated at a level of generality. But that is still a legal test. The section creates a legal standard which must be complied with by a relevant body, and if necessary enforced by a court, which in any given case would, if necessary, be required to determine if any decision or action was consistent, insofar as practicable, with the matters specified in s. 15. 

 79. The difference in the case of an obligation to perform a function " consistent with " , rather than " in compliance with " , a set standard, is that a greater range of options may be said to satisfy the test of consistency. Because of that range of options, the qualification of practicability, and the difference between an individual decision and an objective stated at a high level of generality, it should not be a difficult matter to establish such consistency. That is so particularly where individual action can be shown to be consistent with some planning strategy, which itself can be taken to satisfy the obligation of consistency. If, however, that obligation is thought to impose undue burdens or create administrative delay, or alternatively create an insufficiently demanding standard, it is for the Oireachtas to consider that the Act should be amended. It is not for the courts to dilute either the obligation deliberately placed on relevant bodies or the courts' own duty to ensure compliance with such body's statutory obligations. Courts have no powers to take steps of their own accord to seek to address the climate crisis, no matter what the views of individual judges on this important issue may be, but where the Oireachtas, by legislation, imposes duties and sets standards, then when their jurisdiction is properly invoked, it is emphatically the duty of courts to ensure that those duties are complied with, and those standards met. Other than in a particular case of a challenge to the constitutional validity of legislation, the function of the courts is simply to give effect to what the Oireachtas has prescribed as a legal norm. Here, the Oireachtas has sought to strengthen the nature of climate change obligations imposed on public bodies by amending s. 15(1) (of the 2015 Act) in the manner it did in the 2021 Act. The court's task in any case is to first construe, and then to give effect to, that legislative judgment in the context of a concrete case. 

 80.  The fact that the contentions advanced on behalf of the State and Commission cannot be accepted in their entirety does not lead, however, to the conclusion that the approach of Coolglass and the High Court judge was correct. 

 81. At a fundamental level, there would be greater merit in Coolglass's argument, if s. 15(1) was a standalone provision addressed to planning decisions only; the obligation was to comply with a provision or standard expressed with a degree of precision; there was no other statutory regulation of the planning process; and if planning authorities' decisions took place in a relative vacuum, and without guidance in relation to policy. But that is not the case. It is important to recall that s. 15(1) is not addressed solely, or even primarily, to planning authorities or even to the planning context. Instead, part of the significance of the section is the fact that it is of general application to all relevant bodies and therefore almost all the public sector, and it must be understood and interpreted in that context. 

 82. The consistency obligation is certainly stronger than a " have regard to " obligation but is more flexible and less demanding than a " comply with " obligation. The matters which any relevant body must perform its functions consistently with, are either themselves expressed at a level of generality, such as the furtherance of national climate objectives contained at s. 15(1)(d), or by reference to plans and strategies themselves expressed at a high level of generality. If the national climate objectives contained more granular detail, the consistency obligation would produce a correspondingly narrower range of possible decisions. But it is not suggested, for example, that there is any planning strategy or objective addressed specifically to the question of wind farms in County Laois, or their location or configuration. Indeed, the only objective to which any reference has been made, is that contained in the CAP, which targets the achievement of 9GW of onshore wind power by 2030. The CAP alone runs to more than 400 pages. It does not purport to prescribe in any more detail how that target is to be achieved. And in particular does not purport to give guidance on the issue in this case as to how the proposals for wind power are to be reconciled with other planning consideration. No reference at all was made to the National Long Term Climate Action Strategy, the National Adaptation Plan, or any sectoral adaptation plan. Coolglass accepted that the more generally expressed climate objectives set out at subparagraphs (d) and (e) (furthering the national climate change objective, and mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions and adapting to the effect of climate change in the State) were to be achieved through the mechanism of the plans at (a), (b) and (c). Accordingly, the claim of inconsistency with the s. 15(1) climate objectives was limited to the reference to the general 9GW target for onshore wind power by 2030, and was in essence a contention that section 15 required the grant of permission to any wind farm development. 

 83. The field of planning is subject to detailed statutory regulation establishing and defining the powers and duties of planning authorities, including the Commission, and which are not removed, amended or altered in any way by the section. There is an extensive range of policies in relation to climate change which planning authorities are already obliged to take into account and to which they have regard. They are not dependent on the s. 15(1) obligation in that regard. Accordingly, when considered in respect of a single planning decision, it is important to recognise that the section takes effect in an already very detailed statutory and policy context. The simple three stage process proposed by Coolglass perhaps exhibits the common error of interpreting a section almost exclusively through the prism of the particular dispute giving rise to the litigation in question, and in doing so over-emphasising the role of courts in the achievement of climate objectives. 

 84. The climate objectives set out in s. 15(1) operate at a much higher level of generality than any planning decision, even for a large-scale project such as this. The question of consistency of any individual action by any relevant body with such objectives, is therefore a much more nuanced and layered one. Implementation of the section 15(1)(a), (b) and (c) plans and strategies may involve action at an increasing level of specificity and concretisation (that action itself to be undertaken by bodies to whom s. 15 applies) which in turn sets the context in which a planning decision is made. The question of consistency of an individual planning decision with the s. 15(1) objectives, is much more complex than a traffic light system of climate friendly (go) (unless impracticable) and climate unfriendly (stop). 

 85. The High Court judgment recognised that the simple three step progression of (1) renewal energy projects and (2) consistent with climate goals and leading to (3) the grant of permission unless impracticable, cannot be applied to the obverse case of refusal of permission on climate grounds. The judgment suggested that this was for two reasons. One was displacement - the fact that the project refused here might be allowed elsewhere with, therefore, no climate mitigation benefit, but with the loss of a project with economic and social benefits. This pragmatic approach, however, could not afford a justification for failing to comply with what the judgment itself considered to be an urgent statutory imperative. 

 86. The second reason the judgment gives is more important. It acknowledges that the concept of net zero contemplates a balance between projects, and can encompass some which may be emission generating, but are of particular economic, social, and community advantage, and other projects. Because the national climate objectives are stated as a total global figure, the refusal of permission for a particular project which is said to be climate friendly, and the grant of permission for one which may create greenhouse gases, may still be consistent with the overall achievement of climate targets. A target is a net one to be assessed globally. But if that is so, and it is, the qualified consistency obligation imposed by s. 15(1) cannot be the sole or even principal determinant of the refusal or grant, or grant subject to conditions (subject to practicability) of planning permission. Considerations of proper planning and sustainable development are necessarily taken into account in any decision, and the High Court judgment correctly recognises that emission creating developments may be properly permitted. But if this is so, it undermines the High Court's insistence that a climate positive project must almost always be permitted. 

 87. This can also be illustrated by another example closer to this case. Assume that a particular County Council had designated an entire County as open to wind farm development other than only 10 hectares of high scenic, cultural and amenity value. If we then assume that multiple wind farm developments have already been approved in respect of that County, but an application is subsequently made for permission for a wind farm development in respect of the reserved scenic area. On the approach urged by Coolglass, adopted by the High Court, it appears that permission would nevertheless have to be granted since such a wind farm can be said to be consistent with the achievement of general climate objectives, and there is nothing impracticable in permitting the development. This however would make a nonsense of the elaborate structure established by the 2015 and 2021 Acts, especially when superimposed on the already detailed and nuanced planning regime created by the Planning and Development Act 2000 (as amended). 

 88. Faced with this difficulty Coolglass sought to refine the test contending that impracticability, contemplated legal as well as factual difficulties, and that since planning authorities are obliged to act in accordance with proper planning and sustainable development under s. 34 of the Planning and Development Act 2000, and cannot act ultra vires , a development which would not be consistent with the proper planning and sustainable development would be impracticable in this sense and therefore permission need not, and indeed could not, be granted. On this approach considerations of proper planning and sustainable development would be introduced into the application of the s. 15(1) consistency obligation for planning authorities considering applications for renewable energy projects. 

 89.  This is a variant of the reasoning set out at paragraph 131 of the High Court judgment which is already quoted at paragraph 30 above. It suggests first that there is a strong presumption in favour of the grant of permission in cases such as this, ( "the answer... will almost always be a grant of permission, and is obviously so here" ), but then goes on to suggest that considerations of proper planning and sustainable development can have the effect of leading to a refusal of a permission for a renewable energy project albeit that it must be approached " in an evaluative way that furthers climate goals ". 

 90. It is not clear however what weight is to be given in the balance to planning and sustainable development considerations, although it appears that that balance is weighted heavily in favour of the grant of permission to climate positive projects and the refusal of projects creating emissions. It is also not clear how planning considerations are to be approached in an evaluative way that favours climate goals. The outcome of such a test would likely be the replacement of a sophisticated and already complex and detailed process of assessment by reference to development plans and national policies within the structure of the 2000 Act, by an unclear and unpredictable test, which would likely give rise to uncertainty at the level of planning decisions and (since the test advanced is a legal one said to follow from statute provisions) increase challenges and consequent delay within the planning system generally. 

 91. The approach advanced by Coolglass on this appeal goes somewhat further in seeking to build planning considerations of proper planning and sustainable development into the concept of practicability. That avoids the difficulty of reducing the planning process to a simple traffic light system, but at the price of removing much of the substance and effect from the interpretation of s. 15(1) advanced by Coolglass and accepted by the High Court. The designation of an area in a County Development Plan as open to wind farm development or not, is itself an exercise of proper planning and sustainable development. If the Commission were to accept that the exclusion of the area in this case was consistent with proper planning and sustainable development, then on this approach it would be entitled to refuse permission on the grounds that although consistent with the climate objective, it is impracticable. But if so, then the approach of Coolglass would still lead to the refusal of permission in this case, but now by reference to a vague and necessarily somewhat subjective test. 

  Part VI - The Interpretation of s. 15(1) of the 2015 Act 

  

 92. It follows that the correct interpretation of s. 15(1) lies somewhere between the approach as advocated by the parties in this appeal. It bears repetition and reemphasis, that s. 15(1) is not focused on planning decisions, and still less upon the decisions of courts reviewing such decisions. To be properly understood, it must be recognised that it applies to all the relevant bodies, many of which have no function in the field of planning. That breadth of application is central to the section and the objective it seeks to achieve. As already observed, the different plans and strategies enumerated in s. 15(1)(a) to (e) are stated at a high level of generality, and can be relevant to a very wide range of activities performed by relevant bodies. Even bodies not normally concerned with issues of climate change must still perform their functions so far as practicable in a manner consistent with the s. 15 objectives. 

 93.
