Furthermore, it was accepted by Coolglass that relevant bodies, and courts reviewing their actions, were not required or permitted to make their own assessment as to what is necessary to achieve the objective of mitigating greenhouse gas emissions and adapting to the effect of climate change in the State and contemplated by s. 15(1)(e). Rather, that objective was to be achieved through the mechanism of the implementation of the plans and strategies set out at subparagraphs (a) to (d) of s. 15(1), and the implementation of the other measures set out in the Act. It is important to an understanding of the section (and the Act more generally) that it is intended to operate in a coherent and integrated fashion across the State sector. 

 94. There are a number of features of the terms of s. 15(1) which deserve close attention: 

(a)        the question of performance of " functions " of the relevant body; 

(b)        the question of the obligation imposed by the requirement to do so "in a manner consistent with " the plans set out (a) to (e); and 

(c)        the qualification that the relevant body is to do so " insofar as practicable" . "Functions" 

  

 95. In the case of each relevant body, the question as to the functions it performs to which the s. 15(1) obligation of consistency applies, is a matter of law. A public body can only perform such functions as it is required or permitted to perform by statute. Section 15 does not, therefore, expand the existing functions of a relevant body or create new functions. It is the existing functions of a relevant body that must be performed in a manner consistent with the s. 15 objectives. Section 15 therefore takes effect within the limits of those functions. 

 96. In the case of an application for planning permission, the functions of a planning authority are those set out at s. 34 of the Planning and Development Act 2000, as repeatedly amended and modified thereafter. Section 34(2)(a) provides that when making its decision a planning authority " shall be restricted to considering the proper planning and sustainable development of the area " having regard to a number of matters including guidelines issued by the Minister under s. 28, and where relevant the policy of the Government, the Minister and any other Minister of Government. These are matters which may themselves be the subject of the s. 15 obligation. 

 97. In particular s. 34(2)(a)(i) provides that the planning authority shall have regard to the provisions of the Development Plan. Section 10 of the 2000 Act (substantially reproduced in s. 43 of the Planning and Development Act 2024) sets out the content of the Development Plan, and the making of which is itself the performance of a function by a relevant body to which s. 15(1) also applies. Section 10(2)(n) (as inserted by the Planning and Development (Amendment) Act 2010 and as amended by s. 19(a) of the Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Act 2021) requires the Development Plan to include objectives for:- 

 "The promotion of sustainable settlement and transportation strategies in urban and rural areas including the promotion of measures to - 

 (i) reduce energy demand in response to the likelihood of increases in energy and other costs due to long term-decline and non-renewable resources, 

 (ii) reduce anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions and address the necessity of adaptation to climate change, taking account of the local authority climate action plan (within the meaning of s. 14B of the Climate Action and Low Carbon Development Act 2015) where such a plan has been made for the area in question." 

Section 14B of the 2015 Act (as amended by the 2021 Act) requires that each local authority shall make a local authority climate action plan specifying the mitigation measures and adaptation measures to be adopted that local authority. 

 98. There is no sense therefore in which the s. 15(1) obligation can be said to supplant or override the obligations of a planning authority. A planning authority must continue to perform its functions. As can be seen those functions are already well aligned with national climate objectives, but s. 15(1) is in the nature of a statutory reset, reminding any authority that the performance of its functions, must be, so far as practicable, consistent with climate objectives. 

  "Consistent with" 

  

 99. Next it is apparent that the obligation to act in a manner " consistent with " the climate objectives is a carefully chosen term. It is certainly distinct from, and more demanding than, an obligation to " have regard to " plans or a strategy which it must be remembered is a well-established and frequently analysed formula in planning law and for that matter other fields. See, for example, Delaney v The Personal Injuries Assessment Board & Ors [2024] IESC 10 , and in particular the judgment of Collins J. at paragraphs 101 ff. Indeed, the fact that the 2021 Act continues to use the " have regard to " formula at different points (see e.g., s. 6(11) and s. 6C (10)) makes it clear that the language of " consistent with " was chosen to convey a particular and more demanding obligation. 

 100. Paragraphs 61 - 70 of the High Court judgment contain a detailed analysis of the different types of possible statutory formulae ranging from " have regard to " through " have due regard to " and " comply with to a reasonable standard " to " comply with as far as practicable or possibl e" to an unconditional obligation to " comply with ". Strikingly however, the judgment does not analyse in detail the formula " consistent with " or attempt to place it on the spectrum analysed in those paragraphs. Instead, the judgment appears to treat it as a " comply with " obligation. The judgment concludes at paragraph 70, that the change in s. 15(1) " is clearly a step-change from a mere have-regard-to obligation to a comply-with obligation. That distinction is foundational and not to be minimised or nullified, and nor could it have been inadvertent " (emphasis added). It is certainly clear that the change in s. 15(1) was intended to be a step change from a " have regard to " obligation, but it was, with respect, an error to treat the carefully chosen statutory language here of consistency, as equivalent to an obligation to achieve compliance . 

 101. The language of " consistent with " particularly when contrasted with both " in compliance with " and " have regard to " is instructive, both in expressing the nature of the obligation imposed on the relevant body, and the range of options open to it on the one hand, and the matter with which consistency must be achieved on the other. An obligation to perform a function consistent with certain matters, is more than a process obligation. It does not simply dictate what steps must be taken before a function is performed. It is addressed to the outcome, which must be capable of being demonstrated to be consistent with an identified standard. 

 102. However, the formula implies that there is more than one outcome possible which may satisfy the test. By contrast " compliance with " is more hard edged. There may also be a relationship between the nature of the objective and the manner in which the obligation is framed. It suggests a more granular and specific obligation, and that compliance with such an obligation is a more black and white question. Thus, for example, if an applicable plan, strategy or guideline required that wind farm turbines were to be placed in a specific grid pattern with an equally specific orientation, then compliance will either be achieved or not. Consistency might allow some more leeway but not much. In other cases where the objective is more general it may be more appropriate to require consistency than compliance. It is clear however that while the choice of the language " in a manner consistent with " does look to the outcome of the performance of the relevant function, it also implies that there are a range of possible outcomes open to the relevant body which may satisfy that obligation, and a degree of tolerance in the manner in which this is to be achieved. 

 "In so far as practicable" 

  

 103. The obligation to perform a function consistently with the climate objectives is itself qualified by the phrase " in so far as practicable ". This qualification was introduced by the 2021 Act, and was a deliberate introduction to which effect must be given. It is notable that the language is used elsewhere in the 2021 amendments, which introduced a new section 4(8)(g), s. 4(11), s. 6A(9)(ii)(IV), s. 6B(13) and s. 14B(3) as well as being included in the amendment to s. 15(1) under consideration. It is a term which has been interpreted by the courts on a number of occasions in a variety of different contexts. 

 104. It is important to recognise that this is a qualification of the obligation imposed by s. 15(1). That section could have been phrased as an unqualified obligation of performance of the function in a manner consistent with the s. 15(1) objective. It follows from this, that the section necessarily contemplates that there may be circumstances in which the relevant body may not be required to perform its functions in a manner consistent with the s. 15(1) objectives where it is not practicable to do so. Furthermore, the qualification is to be contrasted with phrases such as " insofar as possible " which is somewhat more demanding. 

 105. O'Donovan v the Attorney General [1961] IR 114, is perhaps the most well-known case in which the concept of practicability has been considered. In that case the High Court was required to interpret Article 16.2.3 of the Constitution which required the ratio of members elected to Dail Eireann to the population in each constituency as ascertained at the last preceding census, to be " so far as it is practicable " the same throughout the country. Budd J. construed the provision as meaning " as far as that is capable of being carried into action in a practical way having regard to such practical difficulties as exist and may legitimately... be taken into consideration ". He agreed with the approach of Goddard L.C.J. in Lee v Nursery Furnishings Limited [1945] 1 All E.R. 387, 389 which adopted the Oxford English Dictionary definition of practicable as capable of being carried out in action or feasible. The term was also considered in the context of insurance in Re Butler [1970] IR 45, in the context of an obligation to post a notice as soon as possible, in the Minister for Agriculture v Kelly [1953] N.I. 151, and in the context of driving offences in Hobbs v Hurley (Costello J., Unreported, High Court, 10 June 1980) where it was stated that in construing the words, the surrounding circumstances and in particular the nature and purpose of the obligation imposed by the statute must be borne in mind. In McC & McD v Eastern Health Board [1996] 2 IR 296, Keane J. was satisfied that these authorities correctly identified the approach which should be taken, and confirmed that as soon as practicable was not to be equated with as soon as possible. More recently the phrase was interpreted in the context of disciplinary proceedings in Gillen v Commissioner of An Garda Síochána [2012] IESC 3 , [2012] 1 IR 574 . 

 106. In the light of this extensive and largely consistent jurisprudence it is unnecessary and potentially unhelpful to attempt any further elaboration of the concept of practicability. It is clear that it is less demanding than " insofar as possible ", and more demanding than " reasonable " and comprehends that something that is capable of being carried into action having regard to such practical difficulties as exist, but does not permit the taking of mere matters of convenience into consideration. It is to be contrasted with phrases such as " insofar as possible ", which are more demanding. It signifies what is practicable in the circumstances and appropriate to the requirements of the situation. 

 107. Putting these components together, and reading s. 15 in its entirety, in its statutory context, and having regard to the obvious purpose of the provision, and reminding ourselves of the key factor that it is intended to, and does apply to the full range of public sector bodies, it is possible to be clearer about its true interpretation. 

 108. Section 15 is not a stand-alone provision. It is not a single radical provision intended to carry the full weight of the State's response to climate change. Rather while not operating at a programmatic level, it does operate within the existing statutory scheme in respect of each relevant body. Accordingly, its impact in any given case, will depend upon the nature and extent of that statutory scheme. It applies to the functions of all relevant bodies, and obliges such bodies to exercise those functions consistently with the climate objectives so far as possible. This operates as a form of climate sense check, and to ensure that decisions and actions of public sector bodies are all aligned with the climate objectives. The section 15(1) obligation is not more prescriptive than that: first because the objective with which consistency is required, is stated at a level of significant generality; second, because consistency implies a range of possible outcomes; and finally, because even that degree of consistency is not required, if it is impracticable. 

 109. It follows that the section does apply at the granular level of an individual planning decision, because that is a function of a relevant body. In that context it may support climate positive planning decisions (whether the grant or refusal or a grant subject to conditions), but it is perhaps less likely that it will have any decisive effect in the field of planning than in the case of other public sector bodies. That is because considerations of climate change mitigation are already woven into the detail of the planning code, sometimes in statute, and sometimes in the detailed strategies, guidelines, and plans, which planning authorities are required to have regard to, or indeed to implement. 

 110. For example, s. 14B of the 2015 Act, (as amended) obliges local authorities to adopt a local authority climate action plan, which, insofar as practicable, is to be consistent with the climate action plan, and the National Adaptation Framework. In this case, as we have seen, the relevant county council had adopted a wind energy strategy. Furthermore, the production by a local authority of a development plan, is now subject to oversight and review by the Minister (s. 31 of the 2000 Act (as amended)) and by the Office of the Planning Regulator OPR (s. 31AM). The latter body is required to endeavour to ensure that the development plan addresses matters generally within s. 10 of the 2000 Act, and in this context, in particular, " subsection 2(n) of that section in relation to climate change ". Furthermore, the development plan, is required to either take account of, or itself be consistent with, policy guidelines and strategies already adopted. Section 15(1) does not introduce climate considerations into the planning process for the first time, and it is very far from being the sole or primary mechanism for ensuring that the planning process generally and any individual planning decision, is consistent with climate change policy. 

 111.  Even without resort to s. 15(1) it would be correct to say that climate considerations permeate the planning process. When it is further recognised that s. 15 itself applies to each of the bodies involved, whether the Minister, the OPR, or a local authority, it becomes clearer that the individual planning decision comes to be made against a background where it is required to have regard to, and is closely aligned to climate policy. While s. 15(1) can be seen as reinforcing that alignment, the circumstances in which the section will have decisive impact will be necessarily limited. 

 112.  It follows that a planning authority is entitled to approach its task on a presumption that any strategy or development plan adopted is consistent with climate objectives, and that any decision consistent with such a plan and strategy will itself be consistent with those objectives, and therefore in compliance with s. 15(1). That is so particularly having regard to the range of outcomes implied by the concepts of consistency, and practicability. 

 113. It is however conceivable that there will be marginal cases where s. 15 may have a significant impact even in the field of individual planning decisions. Coolglass suggested in argument that it would be open for an applicant for planning permission to contend that compliance with a particular development plan would not be consistent with the objectives set down in s. 15(1) and that the Commission, in order to comply with its own obligations under the section, would be obliged to depart from the development plan and exercise its power under s. 37G(6) or, where applicable, s. 37(2). Similarly, since the sequence of production of plans and strategies is not precisely integrated, it is possible that a development plan, which covers a five-year period, may have been drafted by reference to earlier iterations of national climate action plans. It is possible therefore, that a development plan although compliant with the then contemporaneous climate action plan could be out of date and could no longer comply with the current climate action plan, or the long-term climate action framework, or national adaptation framework, or approved sectoral adaptation plan, as the case may be. Again, in such a case s. 15(1) might lead the Commission to use its power to grant permission notwithstanding the material contravention. Finally, at a more individual level, it might also be that the permission sought was itself at the borders of an area designated as not available for such development, or that it can be said that the position proposed was not one which particularly engaged with the values of preservation of areas of scenic or natural beauty which had led to the designation of the area as not available. At the same time, the demands of the climate emergency reflected in the most up-to-date climate action plan might tip the balance in such a case so that permission should be granted. In any of these cases, it can be argued that the duty imposed on the Commission by s. 15(1) should mean that the Commission should exercise its power to grant permission notwithstanding that the development would be a material contravention of the development plan. 

 114. More generally, in most cases it will be the case that a project will be entitled to permission, or to be refused, or to have permission granted with conditions, because of the correct application of considerations of proper planning and sustainable development, which themselves have been shaped by the State's plans and strategies for the achievement of the climate objectives, but s. 15 may reinforce that process, and in some cases be decisive. It follows that in the planning context, s. 15 need not be addressed by a planning authority of its own motion. However, if the section is relied on in support of an application, an authority should be able to explain why the decision to which it has come is consistent as far as practicable with the climate objectives. For the reasons already discussed, that in most if not all cases, ought to be a relatively simple exercise. 

 Application to this Case 

 115. For the reasons set out, while we are of the view that the analysis of s. 15(1) urged by the State cannot be sustained, we are also of the view that a central part of the reasoning of the High Court judge on this question cannot be upheld. The duty on the Commission to perform its function in a manner consistent with the climate objectives set out in s. 15(1), while real, effective, and if necessary enforceable, cannot be converted into a simple formula as proposed by Coolglass and accepted by the High Court. 

 116. Notwithstanding the fact that the developer did not place much emphasis on s. 15(1), we do not consider that the decision of the Commission, and the report of the Inspector on which it relied, is a sufficient or adequate performance of the function of the Commission. The development here clearly involved a material contravention of the development plan. The fundamental question therefore was whether the Commission should exercise its power (under s. 37G (6)), and the obvious and basic argument in favour of it so doing was the climate benefit of the proposed development. It is regrettable that it appears that the Commission in its decision, and the Inspector in his report, did not engage with that question in a real and substantive way and instead and unfortunately, the decision and the report are both phrased in terms that seem to imply that the very fact the development would contravene the development plan was considered itself a good reason to refuse the permission. This was an almost circular reasoning, with the result that the significant climate benefits of the project are not weighed and assessed as a reason for granting permission notwithstanding that it would constitute a material contravention. When this is viewed through the lens of s. 15(1) the conclusion that the Commission's treatment of this issue was both inadequate and incorrect, is reinforced. The Commission's decision did not engage with its power to grant permission in material contravention for a project that amounted to a material contravention of the development plan. This was an error of law which is fatal to the validity of the decision particularly, when viewed in the light of s. 15(1). Accordingly, the decision of the High Court to quash the decision on Core Ground 1, must be upheld, albeit for reasons different from those which led the High Court to that conclusion. 

 117. A final question arises as to whether the matter should be remitted to the Commission, and if so, at what point. It is the provisional view of the Court, that the matter should indeed be remitted to the Commission to consider the question of whether it should exercise its power under section 37G(6) of the Planning and Development Act 2000 (as amended) in the light of s. 15(1) of the 2015 Act (as amended). However, the Court will seek brief submissions from the parties as to the appropriate order to be made in this regard. 

 118. In view of the general importance of this issue it may be useful to summarise our conclusions on this aspect of the case: 

 (i)             The evident purpose and effect of s. 15 of the 2015 Act following the amendments made in 2021, is to strengthen the obligations imposed upon bodies (including the Commission) and to make the performance of all their functions consistent with the climate objectives insofar as is practicable. That obligation is, in principle, enforceable by a court. 

 (ii)          The requirement imposed by s. 15, cannot simply be reduced to a purely procedural obligation, or confined to operation at a programmatic level. Therefore, the provision requires more than that bodies (including the Commission) that are subject to its terms " have regard to " the climate objectives referred to in the section. 

 (iii)        While the language " in a manner consistent with " looks to the outcome of the performance of the relevant function, it also implies that there is a range of possible outcomes open to the relevant body which may satisfy the application, and a degree of tolerance in the manner in which it is achieved. 

 (iv)         That tolerance is further reinforced by the inclusion in s. 15 of the qualification entailed by the words " in so far as practicable " . These make it clear that the section contemplates that there may be circumstances in which a relevant body may not be required to perform its functions in a manner consistent with the s. 15(1) objectives. The decided cases propose that " in so far as practicable " means something that is capable of being carried into action having regard to such practical difficulties that exist, but does not permit the taking of mere matters of convenience into consideration. That qualification is, however, to be contrasted with phrases such as " insofar as possible " , which are more demanding. It comprehends what is practical in the circumstances and appropriate to the requirements of the situation.  

 (v)           Because s. 15(1) applies to all relevant bodies, and the exercise of their functions, the impact in fact of the section will vary depending on the functions of the relevant body, and the matters to which they are obliged to have regard, or to implement. 

 (vi)         The question for a court where it is asserted that the actions of any relevant body failed to comply with s. 15(1), is whether the performance of the functions of the relevant body in that regard falls within the spectrum of possible outcomes that could be said to be consistent, in so far as is practicable, with the objective of s. 15. 

 (vii)      That is a legal test. Section 15 creates a legal standard which must be complied with by a relevant body, and if necessary enforced by courts, which in any given case will be required to determine if any decision or action was in so far as practicable consistent with the matters specified in s. 15. 

 (viii)    Because of the range of options presented by the consistency obligation as so explained - together with the qualification of practicability - and the difference between an individual decision and objective stated at a high level of generality, it should not be a difficult matter to establish such consistency, particularly when the individual action can be shown to be consistent with some plan or strategy which itself was prepared subject to the obligation contained in s. 15(1) or can otherwise be taken to satisfy the obligation of consistency. 

 (ix)         In the field of individual planning decisions, it is perhaps less likely that s. 15(1) will have decisive effect than in respect of the actions of other relevant bodies. That is because the pursuit and achievement of the climate objective is already woven into the planning process to a significant degree. 

 (x)           While it follows that the construction of s. 15 urged by the State parties cannot be accepted, nor can the approach urged by Coolglass. Its interpretation of the provision in the planning context, would result in a strong presumption favouring the grant of permission for any renewable energy project, subject only to considerations of practicability and the exclusion of any other consideration. The question of consistency of an individual planning decision with the s. 15(1) objectives, is much more complex than a traffic light system of climate friendly 'go' (unless impracticable), and climate unfriendly 'stop' . 

 (xi)         By the time a planning decision comes to be made, the manner in which it is proposed the State will meet its climate objectives has been set at a national level, percolating down to a local level through the specific context of the development plan. A planning authority is entitled to commence into consideration with a presumption that compliance with the development plan will itself be compliant with its s. 15(1) duty. 

 (xii)      In the present context, the Commission has a power to grant permission which contravenes the provisions of the development plan under s. 37(2) or s. 37G(6). That is a function of the Commission to which s. 15(1) applies. However, it is not a case of asking whether material contravention of the plan will assist in achieving the climate goals and therefore granting permission for any renewable energy project that does so. The function being exercised is the grant of permission for a development which materially contravenes the development plan. It is this function which must be performed so far as is practicable, consistent with the climate change objectives in s. 15(1). 

 (xiii)    If in such a case, the development plan is itself consistent with the climate objectives set out in s. 15(1), then it will normally be the case that a decision which complies with that plan will itself be consistent with those objectives. However, it may be possible to contend that permission should be granted, because it is established that the development plan does not meet the climate objectives, or no longer does so because of a change in those objectives, or because of particular features of the specific development. In any such case, the Commission must consider whether it should grant the permission, and if the matter is raised, should be able to explain why the decision it has come to is indeed consistent with those objectives. 

 (xiv)     Section 15(1) may also affect the planning process outside the question of any material contravention. In most cases it will be the case that the project will be entitled to permission or will be likely to be refused because of the application of planning considerations which themselves have been shaped by the State's plans and strategies for the achievement of the climate objectives. But s. 15 may reinforce that process. Where but only where it is raised in support of an application, an authority should be able to explain why the decision it has come to is in compliance with s. 15 (1). 

 (xv)       In this case, a central part of the reasoning of the High Court cannot be upheld. The duty on the Commission to perform its function in a manner consistent with the climate objectives set out in s. 15(1), while real, effective and enforceable, cannot be converted into the simple formula advanced by Coolglass and accepted by the High Court. 

 (xvi)     The fundamental question in this case was whether the Commission should exercise its power under s. 37G(6), and the obvious and basic argument in favour of it doing so was the climate benefit of the proposed development. It is not apparent that the Commission ever engaged with that question in a real and substantive way, and instead the decision and report are phrased in terms that seem to imply that the very fact that the development would contravene the development plan was considered itself a reason to refuse the permission. That was an error of law because the Commission was required to consider whether the climate benefits of the project required or justified the grant of permission notwithstanding the material contravention of the development plan. This was reinforced, when considered in light of the s. 15(1) obligation. Accordingly, the decision of the Commission must be quashed, and the decision of the High Court in this regard must be upheld, albeit on different, and narrower grounds. 

   Part VII  The Commission's Reference to the Wrong Statutory Power (Core Ground 4) 

 119. Core Ground 4 involves a related point. It is this: it is said that the Commission acted ultra vires, in that in giving consideration to whether the proposed development would materially contravene the development plan it (and the Inspector) referred to s. 37(2) of the 2000 Act rather than to s. 37G(6). Whereas the former subsection permits the Commission to depart materially from the terms of the development plan if certain conditions are satisfied, the latter provision (which applies only to strategic infrastructure developments) does not specify the circumstances in which the Commission may depart from the terms of the development plan, and accordingly would appear to give the Commission a freer hand in this regard. 

 120. It is accepted that the Commission erred in this respect but it is said in reliance on the comments of Hogan J. in Pembroke Road Association v An Bord Pleanála [2022] IESC 30 , [2022] 2 ILRM 417 (" Pembroke Road Association "), that the decision should nonetheless not be regarded as being intra vires . In Pembroke Road Association the Board had clearly intended that a financial contribution should be levied from a particular developer but had identified the wrong statutory provision for this purpose. As Hogan J. then said ( [2022] 2 ILRM 417 , 435):- 

 " The [ Commission ] sought to rectify this error by amending the condition so as to include the correct reference. This correction does not in any sense materially affect the original permission: it would be different if, for example, the [ Commission ] now sought to amend the condition so as to impose a financial contribution for the first time. 

 It is true that the invocation of an incorrect statutory provision is rather more serious than the commission of a pure clerical error. In some circumstances an error of this kind might so fatally weaken the very integrity of the impugned administrative decision that it would lie beyond the capacity of the remedial provisions of s. 146A [ of the 2000 Act ] to cure. That, however, is not the case here. To repeat, the error here was a purely venial one, not otherwise affecting the integrity of the decision. If the [ Commission ] are correct, the error can readily be corrected by the simple expedient of substituting the correct statutory reference in the planning decision ." 

 121. The error here is somewhat more serious in character than that at issue in Pembroke Road Association . The use of the language of s. 37(2) presupposed that this was an appeal from a planning authority, whereas this was in fact a planning application in respect of a strategic infrastructure development which was designed to be dealt with in the first instance by the Commission. And whereas both statutory provisions empower the Commission to depart, in a material fashion, from the terms of the relevant development plan, s. 37(2) subjects such a decision to certain statutory preconditions which are not present in the case of strategic infrastructure developments considered under s. 37G(6). It follows therefore that this was an error of law which did affect the vires of the Commission's decision. 

 122. The question of whether that decision should be quashed by certiorari is, however, a different one. In the ordinary way a Commission's decision might be set aside in the light of this jurisdictional error of law but the Commission urges, that even if the Court were to otherwise find for Coolglass on the issue of vires , the Court should nonetheless refuse to quash it on two separate discretionary grounds. 

 123. It is first said that this error was, in fact, induced by Coolglass since its submission to the Inspector refers exclusively to the s. 37(2) - and not to the s. 37G(6) - power. Certiorari may be withheld on discretionary grounds if the error was induced by the conduct of Coolglass who now sought to have it quashed on that ground. At a broader level of principle, it is clear that it is not possible to approbate and reprobate by, on the one hand urging ground X on decision maker Y, and then subsequently alleging that decision maker Y had fallen into error by actually adopting ground X. 

 124. A second objection is that the grounds urged by Coolglass as to why the Commission should exercise its s. 37G(6) powers (and wrongly referred to by Coolglass as s. 37(2)) were similar - if not identical - to those already specific grounds which are contained as conditions in s. 37(2), so that it can be said that no real prejudice arises in circumstances by the failure to apply the correct section. While s. 37G(6) is in general terms, it certainly comprehends all the grounds and conditions set out in s. 37(2), any of which if established would be a justification for exercising the power under s. 37G(6). It follows, it is argued by the Commission, that there was no error in considering those issues, which were the issues advanced by Coolglass as entitling it to the grant of permission notwithstanding the material contravention of the development plan, and conversely, it is clear that Coolglass did in fact not advance any ground (and do not now point to any such ground) which would have been admissible under s. 37G(6) but not comprehended by s. 37(2). If therefore, and induced by Coolglass, the Commission took an incorrect view of the extent of its jurisdiction to grant permission, it had no effect in this case because it did not lead to the Commission refusing to consider a ground or issue which it could properly have considered under s. 37G(6). 

 125. There is considerable force in these submissions. In our view, if this ground stood alone as the sole legal flaw in the decision, the Court should not grant an order of certiorari for the reasons urged by the Commission . However, and as already indicated the Commission's decision should be quashed on the more fundamental basis that it failed to properly address the question of the grant of permission notwithstanding that it would amount to a material contravention of the development plan particularly in the light of s. 15(1) of the 2015 Act (as amended). That is a matter going to the heart of the manner in which the Commission discharged its function. By contrast, the reference to the incorrect section was an error which was induced by Coolglass and it was one which did not have any consequence in considering the substance of application made by it. In those circumstances we consider that the Court should not grant certiorari on this particular ground and the High Court's conclusion in this regard should be set aside. 

   Part VIII ­  Whether the Commission Abdicated its Function to the OPR or to the Minister (Core Ground 3) 

 126. The argument here advanced by Coolglass, and accepted by the High Court, was that the Commission had effectively abdicated its powers under s. 15 of the 2015 Act and/or s. 37G(6) of the 2000 Act to the OPR or the Minister, or in having regard to the fact that neither the OPR nor the Minister had exercised their powers in respect of the development plan's designation of areas where wind energy was designated as " not open for consideration ", the Commission had taken into account an irrelevant consideration. 

 127. Coolglass's complaint under this heading was directed at note 2 to the Commission's decision which provides:- 

 " In deciding to refuse permission, the [ Commission ] noted that at policy-making stage the planning authority's Wind Energy Strategy was subject to oversight by the Office of the Planning Regulator and subsequent Ministerial Direction. However, the [ Commission ] noted that the areas designated where wind energy was 'not open for consideration' remained unaltered with regards to the area of the proposed development in the final confirmed and adopted County Development Plan ." 

 In his judgment, the High Court judge concluded (at para. 50) that the fact that the Commission had noted the position of the OPR and the Minister with regard to the excluded area of the development plan, or had not intervened in that regard was a " manifestly irrelevant consideration " and considered that the decision could be quashed on this ground as well. 

 128. If this reference in the Commission's decision could give rise to an extensive and careful decision being quashed on the grounds of taking into account an irrelevant consideration, or on the grounds that the Commission, in considering this matter somehow abdicated its function to other bodies, it would reduce this important jurisdiction of judicial review almost to the level of a legal parlour game. The Oireachtas has established the OPR, and the evaluation and assessment of local development plans is one of the core functions of that office: see s. 31P(1)(a) of the 2000 Act. In this context the OPR is required in discharging its functions to have regard to a range of government policies and public policy objectives (including compliance with EU law) (s.31S of the 2000 Act as amended) and address a range of " legislative and policy matters ": see s. 31AM(2)(e) of the 2000 Act. 

 129. It follows, therefore, that the fact that the OPR had considered Laois County Council's Wind Energy Strategy, and by extension the zoning aspects of its development plan, and had not sought any alteration of them, is necessarily a relevant consideration. All of this bears on the integrity of the development plan system prescribed in the 2000 Act: the adoption of the plan by local councillors (s. 13 of the 2000 Act) and the system of oversight in respect of the plan by the OPR and, ultimately, the Minister. The existence of the OPR is a safeguard to ensure that the development plan is properly aligned with both government policy and legislative requirements, and it underscores the importance of the development plan in the overall planning system. 

 130. If, for example, the OPR had concluded that the development plan's excluded areas were too extensive, or were otherwise inappropriately zoned, this surely would have been a factor to which the Commission might properly have had regard in considering whether to exercise its s. 37G(6) powers to grant permission, notwithstanding the fact that it would constitute a material contravention of the development plan. The converse must equally be correct. It might be different if the Commission had expressed itself as somehow bound by the OPR's conclusion that the development plan should remain unaltered. The Commission's note is, however, no more than an observation that a designation impliedly criticised by Coolglass, had not itself been the subject of adverse comment by another body with a statutory function of reviewing the development plan and its compliance with national policy objectives. That is an observation any person might make in the circumstances and should not be a basis for setting aside a decision as a matter of law. Similarly, it cannot be concluded from this relatively short reference to the OPR that the Inspector or Commission had abdicated its own responsibility to decide the question. This Court has concluded that the Commission's performance of its function was insufficient as a matter of law, but it was the Commission's own error. Accordingly, the appeal in respect of the High Court's finding with regard to Core Ground 3 must be allowed. 

   Part IX ­  Interprétation Conforme and EU Law 

 131. At paragraph 97 of his judgment the High Court judge found that the interpretation of the s. 15(1) power which he favoured, was supported by the conclusion that otherwise Ireland would be in breach of its EU law obligations (including, it seems, the duty of sincere cooperation under Article 4(3) TEU). The judgment explained (at paras. 97-98):- 

 " The problem for the [ Commission ] is that an interpretation of s. 15(1) that allows the [ Commission ] to merely haveregardto climate goals rather than actually comply with such goals would give rise to a failure to give effect to or a jeopardising of the attainment of the objectives of European law, including the binding obligations of the European Union and its member states with respect to climate change, contrary to the duty of sincere cooperation. 

 An interpretation of s. 15 insofar as it applies to the [ Commission's ] decisions on such infrastructure that supports the overall requirement to comply with EU law regarding supply of renewable energy, is consistent with the Marleasing requirement to read domestic law in an EU law-compatible way ." 

 132. The judgment went on to record various failures on the part of Ireland to meet EU climate goals and objectives on renewable energy targets. The High Court judge accepted - as did counsel for Coolglass in this Court - that the 2015 and 2021 Acts were both autochthonous items of domestic legislation which were not designed to give effect to any specific items on European Union law but the judgment did not see this as dispositive of the question (at paras. 100-102):- 

 " The State replies to the effect that the 2015 and 2021 Acts were not in purported transposition of any specific EU law measure. And it [ is ] true that the Acts do [ not ] state on its face that they are transposing any given such measure. It [ is ] also true that EU law does [ not ] , in terms, require member states to impose such an interpretive and general obligation on public bodies. But as the applicant says, this is 'just irrelevant'. The critical point is that faced with an issue of interpretation of a national provision, the domestic courts should give that provision an interpretation that supports and implements EU law rather than allows such law to be undermined. 

 The irrelevance of the point that no specific directive is being implemented by the 2021 Act is borne out by the important relevant principle laid down by the CJEU Grand Chamber in the judgment of 5 October 2004 Pfeiffer joined cases C-397/01 to C-403/01, European Court Reports 2004 I-08835, ECLI:EU:C:2004:584 ." 

 133. This argument was advanced as an aid to the interpretation of s. 15(1) and largely falls away now in the light of this Court's conclusions as to the proper interpretation of that section, and the fact that in its own terms, it cannot be treated either as a compliance obligation (as the High Court seemed to consider) or a " have regard to " obligation. As interpreted by this Court, there is simply no question of any inconsistency with EU law whether specific or general. For the issue to arise at all, it would be necessary to demonstrate that EU law required an approach of a presumption in favour of granting permission in respect of renewable energy projects unless impracticable, and there is simply no basis for this. However, since the judgment sets out an approach to interpretation more generally, it may be helpful to look in more detail at the two judgments of the CJEU relied upon: Marleasing SA v La Comercial Internacional de Alimentacion SA Case C-106/89, European Court Reports [1990] 4 I-4135, ECLI:EU:C:1990:395 (" Marleasing ") and Bernhard Pfeiffer (C-397-01), Wilhelm Roith (C-398-01), Albert Süß (C-399/01), Michael Winter (C-400/01), Klaus Nestvogel (C-401/01), Roswitha Zeller (C-402/01) and Matthias Döbele (C-403/01) v Deutsches Rotes Kreuz (Joined Cases C-397/01 to C-403/01, European Court Reports [2004] I-08835, ECLI:EU:C:2004:584 ) (" Pfeiffer "). 

 134. The decision of the Court of Justice in Marleasing , is of course, regarded as a landmark decision on the principle of interprétation conforme , i.e. the idea that national courts must be prepared to adopt an interpretation of national law:- 

  " as far as possible, in the light of the wording and the purpose of the directive in order to achieve the result pursued by the latter and thereby comply with the third paragraph of Article 189... " (now the third sentence of Article 288 TFEU) (para. 8). 

 135. In the subsequent decision in Pfeiffer the question was whether the provisions of the Working Time Directive applied to certain emergency care workers employed by the German Red Cross. There was no suggestion at all in the judgment that the Red Cross was anything other than a private organisation for this purpose. Although Germany had enacted legislation in 1994 to give effect to the 1994 Directive, it had assumed that the road transport exclusion contained in that directive applied to emergency care workers such as those working in the ambulance service. In the first part of the judgment the Court held that the German legislation had imperfectly transposed the directive because it had (wrongly) assumed that the position of emergency care workers was covered by the exclusion. It next held that the provisions were directly effective. 

 136. The Court of Justice then turned to the question of how the directive should be interpreted by the German Courts. Applying the Marleasing principle, the Court held that (at paras. 115-116):- 

 " Although the principle that national law must be interpreted in conformity with Community law concerns chiefly domestic provisions enacted in order to implement the directive in question, it does not entail an interpretation merely of those provisions but requires the national court to consider national law as a whole in order to assess to what extent it may be applied so as not to produce a result contrary to that sought by the directive. 

 In that context, if the application of interpretative methods recognised by national law enables, in certain circumstances, a provision of domestic law to be construed in such a way as to avoid conflict with another rule of domestic law or the scope of that provision to be restricted to that end by applying it only in so far as it is compatible with the rule concerned, the national court is bound to use those methods in order to achieve the result sought by the directive ." 

 137. The Court further observed at paragraph 117 that the national courts:- 

  " must, when applying the provisions of national law specifically intended to implement the directive, interpret those provisions so far as possible in such a way that they are applied in conformity with the objectives of the directive". 

         This meant that (at paras. 118-119):- 

 " In this instance, the principle of interpretation in conformity with Community law thus requires the referring court to do whatever lies within its jurisdiction, having regard to the whole body of rules of national law, to ensure that Directive 93/104 is fully effective, in order to prevent the maximum weekly working time laid down in Article 6(2) of the directive from being exceeded (see, to that effect, Marleasing , paragraphs 7 and 13). 

 Accordingly, it must be concluded that, when hearing a case between individuals, a national court is required, when applying the provisions of domestic law adopted for the purpose of transposing obligations laid down by a directive, to consider the whole body of rules of national law and to interpret them, so far as possible, in the light of the wording and purpose of the directive in order to achieve an outcome consistent with the objective pursued by the directive . In the main proceedings, the national court must thus do whatever lies within its jurisdiction to ensure that the maximum period of weekly working time, which is set at 48 hours by Article 6(2) of Directive 93/104, is not exceeded " (emphasis added). 

 138. It is clear from the facts of Pfeiffer and indeed the passage emphasised above, that that case concerned the application of the Marleasing principle to the interpretation of national law designed to give effect to a specific directive. The key point is that Pfeiffer is not an authority for the proposition that there is some wider and more general principle of interpretation whereby national laws are to be interpreted by reference to EU law in a context other than those particular instances where the national law in question is designed to give effect to a specific EU legislative obligation. It is in those latter instances alone - where the national court is called upon where necessary to give that national law a Marleasing style interpretation - that this general principle of interprétation conforme applies. 

 139. In this Court, Coolglass did not seek to stand over the findings of the High Court (para. 159) that the State was in breach of its duty of sincere cooperation under Article 4(3) TEU. It did however seek to pray this principle in aid of the general method of interpretation of s. 15(1) of the 2015 Act (as amended). When pressed as to what authority there might be for this wider proposition, counsel for Coolglass was obliged to fall back exclusively on Pfeiffer . Yet Pfeiffer is concerned solely with the obligation to adopt an interprétation conforme in the context of a national law designed to give effect to a binding EU legislative instrument such as a directive. It is not authority for any wider proposition. 

 140. Accordingly, Coolglass's argument on the EU law ground (Core Ground 7) must be rejected. The Court would also set aside the finding in the High Court that the State was in breach of its obligation of sincere cooperation contrary to Article 4(3) TFEU. 

 Part X ­  Breach of Council Regulation (EU) No. 2022/2577 (Core Ground 6) 

 141. Council Regulation (EU) 2022/2577 ("the 2022 Regulation") was adopted on 22 December 2022. It prescribes a temporary framework designed to accelerate the deployment of renewable energy, specifically the grant of planning permission in respect of renewable energy projects and related grid infrastructure. The Regulation expired on 30 June 2024 but some of its revisions were extended to 30 June 2025 by amending Regulation (EU) 2024/223. 

 142. As Recital 1 of 2022 Regulation makes clear, this temporary provision was prompted by the:- 

 " Russian Federation's war of aggression against Ukraine and the unprecedented reduction of natural gas supplies from the Russian Federation to Member States threaten the security of supply of the Union and its Member States ". 

 143. The entire objective of the legislation is to accelerate the deployment of renewable energy. It does so by rebalancing the legal interests, and creating a new presumption in favour of renewable energy targets in the context of carrying out certain assessments for the purposes of Article 6(4) and Article 16(1)(c) of the Habitats Directive (Council Directive 92/43/EEC), and Article 4(7) of the Water Framework Directive (2000/60/EC) and Article 9(1)(a) of the Birds Directive (2009/147/EC). 

 144. The High Court judge rejected the application on these grounds saying (at para. 156), that the issue did not really arise on the facts because the basis of the refusal was contravention of a development plan, not impacts on European sites. Subsequent to the Supreme Court hearing, Coolglass notified the Court that it was no longer relying on this particular ground of appeal. In these circumstances it is not necessary to examine this point. 

   Part XI ­  Alleged Breach of Article 8 ECHR (Core Ground 5) 

 145. It is necessary to turn finally to the finding of the High Court that the Commission was in breach of its Article 8 ECHR obligations by reference to s. 3 of the 2003 Act. It was contended, and held by the High Court, that the Commission had breached its s. 3 obligation by failing to exercise its discretionary power under s. 37G(6) to grant a permission in this case. 

 146. On this point the judge first noted that the ECtHR had delivered judgment in KlimaSeniorinnen . He continued (at paras. 107-108):- 

             " The judgment contains a wide overview of developments in climate law and litigation. The court found a violation of art. 8 of the ECHR which encompasses a right to effective protection from the serious adverse effects of climate change. There was a breach of the positive obligations thereby imposed in terms of establishing a relevant domestic regulatory framework relating to budgeting for and limiting emissions. In addition, the failure by the domestic courts to accept the applicants' standing to litigate was a breach of art. 6.1 of the ECHR 

 For present purposes, there are two pertinent elements to the KlimaSeniorinnen case - putting in place a framework of measures and complying with that framework : 

             ' 550. When assessing whether a State has remained within its margin of appreciation... the Court will examine whether the competent domestic authorities, be it at the legislative, executive or judicial level, have had due regard to the need to: 

             (a) adopt general measures specifying a target timeline for achieving carbon neutrality and the overall remaining carbon budget for the same time frame, or another equivalent method of quantification of future GHG emissions, in line with the overarching goal for national and/or global climate-change mitigation commitments; 

             (b) set out intermediate GHG emissions reduction targets and pathways (by sector or other relevant methodologies) that are deemed capable, in principle, of meeting the overall national GHG reduction goals within the relevant time frames undertaken in national policies; 

             (c) provide evidence showing whether they have duly complied, or are in the process of complying, with the relevant GHG reduction targets (see sub-paragraphs (a)‑(b) above); 

             (d) keep the relevant GHG reduction targets updated with due diligence, and based on the best available evidence; and 

             (e) act in good time and in an appropriate and consistent manner when devising and implementing the relevant legislation and measures. " 

 147. The High Court then concluded by saying (paras. 109-115):- 

 " I agree with the applicant that one must conclude that art. 8 of the ECHR imposes a positive obligation on the State to put in place a legislative and administrative framework with respect to climate change designed to provide effective protection of human health and life, and a further positive obligation to apply that framework effectively in practice, and in a timely manner. 

             Ireland has a framework of course but (as discussed above under the heading of EU law conformity) it is clear that it is not being complied with. The latter failure, on the logic of KlimaSeniorinnen , involves a breach of art. 8 of the ECHR. 

             The application of the framework in practice is crucial. As we know from the termination of pregnancy context ( Case of A, B and C v. Ireland [GC], no. 25579/05, ECHR 2010), the Strasbourg court takes a dim view of a situation where there are laws on the books but a failure to put in place practical arrangements to implement them. 

             The problem for the opposing parties here is firstly that an interpretation of s. 15(1) that allows the climate goals in legislation to fall by the wayside due to a failure by the [ Commission ] to exercise discretionary powers to override development plans is an interpretation that fails to conform with ECHR obligations contrary to s. 2 of the 2003 Act. 

             Secondly, the failure by the [ Commission ] to use its discretionary powers in that manner constitutes a failure to act consistently with ECHR obligations contrary to s. 3 of the 2003 Act. 

             The [ Commission ] rather weakly raises the defence that a body corporate does [ not ] have locus standi to argue for the right to a private life in a climate-relevant sense under art. 8 of the ECHR. But that is [ not ] the point of course. Whether an individual applicant has standing in a hypothetical case or not does [ not ] affect the interpretation of a statutory provision. The point being made is that the court should interpret the 2015 Act as amended in an ECHR-compatible manner. Such an interpretation supports the applicant's proposition that s. 15(1) should be read as meaning what it says. 

             Thus the requirement to read legislation in an ECHR-compliant manner supports an interpretation of s. 15 that goes beyond the [ Commission's ] have-regard-to interpretation and the State's meaningful engagement interpretation. It reinforces the applicant's case that the interpretation should ensure that ECHR obligations are complied with in practice, including compliance in practice with stated goals in relation to renewable energy infrastructure ." 

 148. It is important to note that in its judgment in KlimaSeniorinnen , the ECtHR had concluded (at para. 573), that it was the systemic failures of the Swiss Confederation which led to the Article 8 ECHR violation. It was on this basis however that the High Court made a finding that the Commission failed to perform its statutory obligations in a manner compatible with the State's obligations under Article 8 ECHR. On its face, the decision of the High Court would appear to represent a significant expansion of the jurisprudence of the ECtHR. This is only one of the very significant issues that would arise for consideration if it appeared that the ECHR issue was likely to be decisive in this case. 

 149. KlimaSeniorinnen is a significant case in the European jurisprudence and may call for careful consideration in an appropriate case. However, the significance of the invocation of KlimaSeniorinnen has greatly receded during the currency of this appeal. In the first place, as already set out, Coolglass no longer seeks to stand over a finding of a separate breach of the ECHR as implemented in Irish law by the 2003 Act. Second, insomuch as reliance was still placed upon the ECHR and the KlimaSeniorinnen case, it was in the much more limited context of contending that it supplied an additional vector leading to the interpretation for which Coolglass contended, and which had been upheld by the High Court. Without unduly simplifying matters, this seemed ultimately to amount to little more than the contention that the interpretation of the Convention adopted in KlimaSeniorinnen was one which supported measures directed to achieving climate goals and that this was consistent with the interpretation of s. 15 urged by Coolglass . In the light of the interpretation of s. 15(1) as outlined by this Court, that argument no longer arises. It cannot in any event be contended that anything in the KlimaSeniorinnen case could be said to require such an interpretation of s. 15(1) such that the Commission when faced with an application for a renewable energy project was obliged to grant permission unless it was impracticable to do so. In these circumstances it is appropriate to make only a limited number of comments on the conclusions of the High Court on the ECHR issue. 

 150. First, as already mentioned, the High Court finding was made against the Commission and not Ireland. The complaint here is against the Commission exclusively by reason of its alleged breach of its obligations under s. 3 of the 2003 Act. That is relevant, because the conclusions in KlimaSeniorinnen were addressed to a perceived systemic failing of the Swiss Confederation in respect of climate change at national, legislative and administrative levels, including matters such as national legislative limits on the production of greenhouse gas emissions and its persistent failure to meet those GHG emissions targets. Nothing similar can be said, or was advanced, in this case. While the matter was not addressed in the detail which would be required if a conclusive finding was to be made, it would appear that the Climate Action Plan and other plans and policies referred to in s.15(1) would seem to be in compliance with the first part of the decision in KlimaSeniorinnen . The evidence relied on for determining that Ireland was not on course to achieve its climate goals was drawn, in part, at least from the Climate Action Plan itself and there was no, or no sufficient evidence, that the objectives of the plans were not being pursued or capable of being achieved. This is in contrast to the particular situation which applied in Switzerland at the time of the KlimaSeniorinnen proceedings. Furthermore it is a significant distance from the finding in that case to a conclusion that the Commission had itself breached Article 8 ECHR by refusing to grant planning permission in this particular case. Third, the ECtHR expressly reserved the question of whether a right to life under Article 2 ECHR had been infringed in that case. By contrast, the High Court appears to have found that there was a breach of this provision, and by the Commission as well. This is perhaps a matter of detail given the separate finding of an Article 8 ECHR violation, but it shows the need for care in the application of the KlimaSeniorinnen judgment. 

 151. Fourth, the ECtHR denied standing to four individual complainants but nonetheless accepted the locus standi of the applicant Association on the ground that the campaigning on climate change grounds was a declared objective of the Association and that it had in fact genuinely done so. The Court recognised that in order to ensure the effective protection of individual rights under Article 8 it was necessary to have an accommodating standard of what constitutes a " victim " for the purposes of Article 34 ECHR. 

 152. It is not necessary for this Court to express any concluded view of this aspect of the case. However, it is not at all obvious that a legal person such as Coolglass, which has been incorporated for ordinary commercial purposes, can be said to fit into the exceptional category of " victim " for the purposes of Article 34 on the grounds that its right to family life under Article 8 ECHR has been infringed. The Association deemed to have standing in KlimaSeniorinnen was a non-profit organisation with an acknowledged record of campaigning on climate change and human rights grounds and which had previously sought to litigate the precise issue before the Swiss Courts. 

 153. These aspects of KlimaSeniorinnen do not appear to feature in the High Court judgment, in part because this aspect of the case appears to have been decided on the basis that the issue was one of interpretation, and the interpretation of s. 15(1) advanced by Coolglass was required by s. 2 of the 2003 Act, in order to ensure that the Irish legislation was compatible with the Convention. Once that interpretation was established, it was said Coolglass was entitled to benefit from it. However, in circumstances where it has (a) not been established that the Convention requires an interpretation of s. 15(1) requiring the grant of permission in this case (absent a showing of impracticability) and (b) where it cannot be said that the interpretation adopted by s. 15(1) set out earlier in this judgment is in any way incompatible with the provisions of the Convention as interpreted in the KlimaSeniorinnen case, it is sufficient to observe that it must be doubtful that Coolglass could claim to be a victim for the purposes of the Convention, or that the requirement to establish such a status could be circumvented in this way when the obligation on organs of the State under s. 3 of the 2003 Act is to perform their functions in a manner compatible with the State's obligations under the Convention provisions. 

 154. In addition to these matters going to the substance of the jurisprudence of the ECtHR, it is necessary to remind ourselves that the ECHR is incorporated in Irish law pursuant to the provisions of the 2003 Act. It has been repeatedly emphasised since the decision of this Court in McD v L [2009] IESC 81, [2010] 2 IR 199 , that any argument by reference to the ECHR should not assume that the Convention takes effect of its own force in Irish law and still less that a court should approach any claim as if it were exercising the jurisdiction of the ECtHR. It is necessary in any given case to explain whether reliance is placed on the interpretive obligation under s. 2 or the obligation on organs of the State to perform their functions in a Convention compliant manner, and if so, what consequences follow. In either case the obligation is to interpret the law or perform a function "in a manner compatible with the State's obligations under the Convention provisions ". This places an important constraint on the powers of a court, and sets the lens through which any such claim is to be assessed. Furthermore, it would normally be expected that where issues of interpretation (or application) of the Convention arise, that issues would equally, if not more directly, arise under the Constitution. The claim advanced in KlimaSeniorinnen relied on Article 8's protection of family life, something protected, if anything, more forcefully under Article 41 of the Constitution. The question of a derived right to a clean environment had, moreover, already been addressed by this Court in Friends of the Irish Environment . If the questions of the impact of climate change on the rights of parties were to be comprehensively addressed it is difficult to understand how those rights could be analysed without reference to the Constitution, or, for that matter this Court's decision in Friends of the Irish Environment . 

 155. However, for reasons already touched on, none of these issues were reached in this case, or on the argument as it developed in this Court, required to be determined. It is sufficient to say on this aspect of the case that while it is apparent that KlimaSeniorinnen is a significant decision in the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights, it is of very limited application, if any, in this case. In any case where it could properly be said to arise, it is to be expected, that it would be carefully analysed, and it is also to be expected, that an argument would be addressed to the provisions of the Constitution consistent with the fact that the Act aims to give further effect to the ECHR, " subject to the Constitution ". 

   Part XII  Conclusion 

 156. The Core Grounds other than Core Ground 1 can be dealt with together as follows:- 

 (a)    Core Ground 3: the Court does not consider that the Commission abdicated its obligations under s. 15 of the 2015 Act either to the Office of the Planning Regulator or the Minister for Local Government and Heritage, or that in referring to the fact that neither the OPR nor the Minister had intervened in relation to the designation of areas as not open for consideration, the Commission had taken into account an irrelevant consideration. In reference to the OPR, and the High Court's finding in this regard cannot be sustained; 

 (b)   Core Ground 4: the Commission did err by placing reliance on s. 37(2) of the 2000 Act instead of s. 37G(6) of the 2000 Act. However, in circumstances where this error followed from an erroneous submission made by Coolglass, and where it has not been demonstrated that this led to any failure to consider a ground for material contravention announced by Coolglass, the Court is not disposed to grant an order of certiorari quashing the decision on this ground, and the finding of the High Court in this regard is set aside; 

 (c)    Core Ground 5: The Commission did not fail to exercise its function in a manner compatible with Articles 2 and 8 ECHR in accordance with s. 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights 2003 Act in the light in particular of the decision in KlimaSeniorinnen; 

 (d)   Core Ground 6: this ground was withdrawn as a ground of appeal; 

 (e)    Core Ground 7: the Commission did not breach its duty of sincere cooperation under Article 4(3) TEU by refusing to exercise its discretion under s. 37G(6) and/or s. 37(2)(b) of the 2000 Act. 

 (f)     Core Ground 1: the Commission did fail in its obligations to consider whether permission should be granted notwithstanding that it would amount to a material contravention of the development plan, particularly having regard to its duty under s. 15(1) of the 2015 Act (as amended by s. 17 of the Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Act 2021). The section creates a legal obligation binding upon the Commission and enforceable, if necessary, by action, to ensure that any decision it makes to grant or refuse permission is consistent with the climate objectives set out in s. 15. The High Court's conclusion that the decision of the Commission to refuse permission was invalid and should be quashed, is accordingly upheld on this basis, but for reasons other than those upon which the High Court based its conclusion. This Court's reasons are summarised at paragraph 118 above. On this basis, the appeal will be dismissed and the order of the High Court quashing the decision of the Commission of 23 August 2024, refusing permission for Coolglass's wind farm development, is upheld. The Court will remit the matter to the Commission having received submissions from the parties as to the point in the process to which the matter should be remitted. 

 Result:     Dismiss Appeal
